title: The Oceans in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe the world ocean and why all life depends on it.
summary: Earth has one connected ocean covering more than 70% of the surface and holding about 97% of its water. It makes about half our oxygen and feeds our rain.

cards.headline: Take a deep breath. The ocean made about half of it.
cards.body: You might live hundreds of kilometers from the nearest beach, and the sea still reaches you, in every breath and every rain shower. Meet the biggest thing on the planet, and find out why nothing alive can do without it.

cards.headline: One ocean, many names
cards.body: A globe shows a Pacific, an Atlantic and more. But NOAA, the US ocean agency, says there is only one global ocean. The names mark regions of it, divided by lines people drew, not by walls of land. That one ocean covers more than 70% of Earth's surface and holds about 97% of all Earth's water. Every lake, river, glacier and cloud on the planet shares the leftovers.
cards.callout: One connected ocean · about 97% of Earth's water

mascot.line: Next time someone says they need some sea air, you can tell them they already have it.

cards.fact: About half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean.
cards.context: It's made by plankton: drifting plants, algae and some bacteria that photosynthesize, soaking up sunlight and giving off oxygen. So when you thank a forest for fresh air, save some thanks for the sea. Roughly every other breath you take is on the ocean's tab.

cards.headline: The ocean waters the land
cards.body: The ocean supplies most of the water that evaporates into the air. Winds carry that vapor, sometimes far inland, and it falls again as rain and snow. The river you cross and the crops you eat all run on that rain and snow. The ocean is the planet's water tank, and the sky is the delivery van.

title: The Blue Planet
objective: After this level you can explain how much of Earth is ocean and how deep it goes.
summary: Water covers about 71% of Earth. The ocean averages about 3,700 m deep, about 11 km at its deepest, yet on a 30 cm globe it would be under 0.1 mm deep.

cards.headline: In 1972, astronauts looked back and saw a blue marble.
cards.body: On December 7, 1972, the Apollo 17 crew, on their way to the Moon, photographed the whole Earth at once. The picture became known as the Blue Marble. Why so blue? And how deep does all that blue actually go?

cards.headline: Seven parts in ten
cards.body: The marble is blue because most of it is water: about 71% of Earth's surface, with the ocean alone covering more than 70%. Spin a globe, stop it with a finger, and most of the time you'll land in the sea. From space, the land is the exception, not the rule.

cards.fact: The ocean is about 3,700 m deep on average.
cards.context: NOAA puts the average at about 3,682 m. That's across the whole ocean: under a typical patch of open sea, there's more than three and a half kilometers of water between you and the bottom. Holding your breath won't cut it.

mascot.line: The deepest place on Earth, reduced to a scratch on a desk globe. Perspective is a wonderful thing.

cards.headline: Deep, and yet thin
cards.body: Now zoom out. Earth's radius is about 6,371 km, so shrink the planet to a globe 30 cm across and the average ocean becomes less than a tenth of a millimeter deep. Even the deepest known spot, Challenger Deep at about 11 km, would be a scratch about a quarter of a millimeter deep. The blue in the Blue Marble is a very thin coat of paint.

cards.headline: The ocean drawn by a current
cards.body: Historically there were four named oceans: the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian and Arctic, each defined by the continents around it. The Southern Ocean is different. It is defined by a current that flows all the way around Antarctica, and its northern edge is set at 60° south. Its border is a line through moving water. Good luck putting up a fence.

cards.headline: Five oceans, one asterisk
cards.body: The US Board on Geographic Names has used the name Southern Ocean since 1999, NOAA counts it as the fifth ocean, and National Geographic began recognizing it on June 8, 2021. The International Hydrographic Organization, which publishes the standard limits of oceans and seas, dropped it in 1953. In 2023 it voted to recognize it again, while leaving each member country free to keep its own view. So: five oceans, most of the time.

title: Where Earth's Water Came From
objective: After this level you can explain the leading ideas for where Earth's water came from.
summary: Deuterium is water's origin clue. Asteroid meteorites match Earth; comet 67P seemed not to, until 2024. Some water came from within Earth. The shares are debated.

cards.headline: Earth was born too hot to keep its water. Or was it?
cards.body: For a long time, scientists thought any water on the newborn Earth would have boiled off or blown away into space, so the oceans must have arrived later, on comets or icy asteroids. So who delivered the sea? The answer is still being argued over.

cards.headline: A fingerprint in every drop
cards.body: Water carries a clue. Its hydrogen comes in two kinds: ordinary hydrogen, and a rare, heavier form called deuterium. Deuterium forms more readily in cold places far from the Sun, so the share of it in water hints at where that water formed. The test is simple: find a space rock whose water has the same fingerprint as your bathtub.

items.label: Comets
points: 2014: ESA's Rosetta measures comet 67P
Its water has more than three times Earth's deuterium ratio
Verdict then: comets like it are unlikely suppliers

items.label: Asteroids
points: Meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites carry water
Their hydrogen fingerprint matches Earth's
A 2014 WHOI-led study: Earth got its water early from such bodies

mascot.line: A cold case with three suspects and no confession. Science at its most honest.

cards.headline: Case reopened
cards.body: In 2024, a NASA-led team found that dust had skewed Rosetta's readings, and that 67P's water looks much like Earth's after all. A 2020 study added a twist: meteorites like the stuff Earth formed from hold enough hydrogen to supply at least three times the water in the oceans. Today's picture is a mix. Some water came from inside Earth, vented by volcanoes, and much came from asteroids and possibly comets. How much from each is still debated.

title: Why the Sea Is Salty
objective: After this level you can explain where the salt in seawater comes from.
summary: Seawater is about 35 parts per thousand salt, mostly chloride and sodium. Rain weathers rock, rivers carry the salt, evaporation leaves it, and vents add more.

cards.headline: Dry out the ocean and the leftover salt would bury every continent.
cards.body: Spread the ocean's salt evenly over all the land and it would form a layer about as tall as a 40-story office building. That's a lot of seasoning. Where did it all come from? Mostly from rocks on land.

cards.fact: Seawater is about 35 parts per thousand salt.
cards.context: In other words, dissolved salts make up about 3.5% of its weight. Most of it is chloride and sodium, the same two ingredients as table salt. That's why a gulp of sea tastes like a kitchen accident.

cards.headline: Rivers deliver, the sea keeps
cards.body: Rain holds a little dissolved carbon dioxide, which makes it slightly acidic, so over time it breaks down rocks on land. Streams and rivers carry the freed salts to the sea. River water has salt in it too, just far too little to taste. At sea, water evaporates but the salt is left behind, so delivery after delivery, it builds up. The river passes the salt along; the ocean hangs on to it.

cards.headline: Salt from below
cards.body: Rivers aren't the only suppliers. On the sea floor, seawater seeps into cracks, is heated by magma and gushes back out of hydrothermal vents carrying dissolved minerals. Undersea eruptions release minerals straight into the water too. So the ocean is salted from both ends: from the land above and the rocks below.

title: Layers of Water
objective: After this level you can explain how temperature and salt stack seawater in layers.
summary: Cold and salty water is denser than warm and fresh, so the sea stacks itself: light water on top, dense below, with the thermocline's quick drop between.

cards.headline: A liter of seawater weighs about 26 g more than a liter of fresh water.
cards.body: That small difference is enough to sort the whole ocean into layers, like a drink that refuses to mix.

cards.headline: Two ways to get heavier
cards.body: Water gets denser in two ways. Cool it down: cold water is denser than warm water. Add salt: salty water is denser than fresh water. At 10°C, a liter of fresh water weighs 1,000 g and a liter of seawater about 1,026 g. So the heaviest water in the sea is the cold, salty kind, and the lightest is warm and fresh.

cards.headline: The ocean sorts itself
cards.body: When waters of different density meet, the ocean orders them: the lighter water rides near the surface and the denser water settles at depth. It's like oil floating on vinegar in a salad dressing, except here both layers are water. Warm water floats on top, and cold, dense water fills the deep.

mascot.line: Warm on top, cold below, and a sharp step between. The ocean keeps its layers neater than my desk.

cards.headline: The thermocline: a cold step down
cards.body: Between the warm, well-mixed surface water and the much colder deep water sits the thermocline, a layer where the temperature drops fast as you go down. It isn't the same everywhere. It's semi-permanent in the tropics, shifts with the seasons in temperate seas, and is shallow or missing altogether in polar seas.

title: Why the Ocean Is Blue
objective: After this level you can explain why seawater looks blue.
summary: Water absorbs red light and scatters blue, so deep water looks blue while a glass looks clear. Sky reflection adds only at the surface; particles and plankton turn it green.

cards.headline: Scoop a glass from the bluest sea on Earth. The water is clear.
cards.body: Pour it back, and it's blue again. So which is it? Both. Water has a faint blue color of its own, far too faint to see in a glass. You need a lot of it.

cards.headline: Water eats the red
cards.body: Sunlight is a mix of every color. When it enters the sea, water absorbs the colors at the red end of the spectrum much more strongly than blue. Like a filter, it strips out reds and oranges and scatters the leftover blue back toward your eyes. The ocean isn't painted blue. It's blue because of what it takes away.

cards.headline: But isn't it just the sky?
cards.body: Partly, right at the surface. The sea does reflect the sky, which is why a big stretch of water looks gray on an overcast day. But the color of the sea and the color of the sky arise separately. The deep blue comes from water absorbing red light, the same reason a glass of it looks clear while a whole sea looks blue.

cards.headline: When the sea turns green
cards.body: Not every sea is blue. Where the water carries lots of sediment and particles, light bounces off them and the sea can look green or other colors. Where phytoplankton are plentiful, their chlorophyll absorbs some colors and tints the water green. A green sea isn't broken. Often it's just crowded.

title: Light Fades Below
objective: After this level you can explain how sunlight fades with depth.
summary: Colors fade in order: red first, blue last. Below about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis, and below 1,000 m no sunlight at all.

cards.headline: Take a red fish 100 m down and it turns black.
cards.body: Nothing happened to the fish. At 100 m there's no red light left to bounce off it, so it looks blackish. Sunlight doesn't just dim as you sink. It loses its colors, one by one.

cards.headline: Colors switch off in order
cards.body: Remember Level 7: water absorbs red light most strongly. So a few meters down, most of the red and orange is already gone. Next to fade are yellow and green. Blue and violet travel deepest of all. That's why the underwater world turns bluer and bluer the deeper you go.

cards.fact: Below about 200 m, there isn't enough light for photosynthesis.
cards.context: Faint light can still be detected as deep as 1,000 m, but past about 200 m there's rarely any significant light, far too little to power anything that makes food from sunlight. So the ocean's sunlight-powered food makers all live near the top.

mascot.line: Most of the ocean has never had a sunny day. Bring a flashlight, and maybe a sweater.

cards.headline: The dark majority
cards.body: Below 1,000 m, no sunlight arrives at all. Now remember Level 2: the ocean averages about 3,700 m deep. So under a typical patch of sea, the floor lies about 2,700 m below the last glimmer of daylight, nearly three quarters of the way down in total darkness. The ocean is mostly a place where the Sun has never shone.

title: Pressure
objective: After this level you can explain how water pressure grows with depth.
summary: Every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure. Water barely squeezes but air does, so deep pressure shrinks a foam cup for good.

cards.headline: Send a foam cup to the deep sea and it comes back doll-sized.
cards.body: Oceanographers decorate foam cups and send them down with their deep-sea gear. The cups come back shrunken, and they stay that way. Nothing touched them but water. So what squeezed them?

cards.headline: A weight that stacks up
cards.body: The answer is pressure. At the surface, the air above you already presses on you with one atmosphere. Every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere more. So at just 10 m down, the pressure on a diver is double what it is at the surface. You don't have to go deep to feel the ocean leaning on you.

cards.headline: Counting atmospheres
cards.body: Keep going and the atmospheres pile up in a steady stack. Water adds about 10 atmospheres at 100 m, and about 200 at 2,000 m. The rule is simple arithmetic: divide the depth in meters by 10, and you have the pressure the water adds, in atmospheres. Easy to count. Much harder to survive.

cards.headline: Why the cup shrinks
cards.body: Water itself barely squeezes, but air does. Foam is full of tiny air pockets, and deep-sea pressure crushes them, so the cup shrinks and never bounces back. Your lungs and the air spaces in your head are air pockets too, and enough pressure would collapse them. That shrunken cup is a warning in miniature.

title: Checkpoint: The Blue Planet
objective: After this level you can describe the size, saltiness and layers of the ocean.
summary: All Earth's water would make a ball about 1,385 km across. Dive in: warm over cold, colors fade, light ends at 1,000 m, pressure climbs. Salty all the way down.

cards.headline: Every drop of water on Earth would fit in a ball smaller than the Moon.

cards.fact: All of Earth's water would make a ball about 1,385 km across.

cards.headline: Take the plunge

cards.headline: Salty all the way down
cards.body: Every liter of that dive is salty: about 35 parts per thousand, mostly chloride and sodium, washed off the land by rivers and pushed up through sea-floor vents. Cold, salty water is dense, which is why it settles into the deep while warm water rides on top. Size, salt and layers: that's the blue planet in one dive.

title: Mapping the Sea Floor
objective: After this level you can explain how sonar mapped the ocean floor.
summary: Light can't reach the deep floor, so it's mapped with sound: first lead lines, then sonar echoes from the 1920s and multibeam fans from the 1960s. As of April 2026, 28.7% was mapped.

cards.headline: We have better maps of Mars than of the floor of our own ocean.
cards.body: That's the U.S. Geological Survey's verdict. The reason: light can't get through deep seawater, so the tools that map land from above can't see the bottom. So how do you map a floor you can't see? You listen for it.

cards.headline: One rope, one number
cards.body: In the early 1800s, sailors measured depth with a lead line: a weighted rope lowered over the side until it hit bottom. Each drop gave the depth at a single point, so charting even a harbor was slow, laborious work. Now remember Level 2: the ocean averages about 3,700 m deep. Mapping a whole ocean floor one rope at a time was never going to happen.

mascot.line: Next time you hear an echo, you're doing a tiny bit of oceanography.

cards.headline: Ping, then wait
cards.body: Sonar, developed in the 1920s, swapped the rope for sound. A ship sends a sound down and times how long its echo takes to bounce back off the bottom: the longer the wait, the deeper the floor. It works where light fails because sound travels far through seawater. Remember Level 8: no sunlight at all reaches below 1,000 m. The deep floor gets mapped by ear, not by eye.

cards.headline: A fan of sound, and a deadline
cards.body: In the 1960s came multibeam sonar: many beams of sound at once, fanned out to map a wide strip under the ship and out to each side. Even so, when the Seabed 2030 project launched in 2017, only about 6% of the ocean floor had been mapped in modern detail. By April 2026, it had reached 28.7%. The goal is all of it by 2030. That's a lot of lawn left to mow.

title: Continental Shelves
objective: After this level you can describe the shallow shelves around the continents.
summary: Continents run on underwater as shallow, nearly flat shelves, usually 100 to 200 m deep, ending at the shelf break. They cover about 8% of the ocean but, sunlit and fed by rivers, teem with life.

cards.headline: Off Siberia, the continent carries on 1,500 km out to sea.
cards.body: The beach isn't where a continent ends. Its edge runs on underwater as a shallow ledge, and off Siberia that ledge stretches about 1,500 km into the Arctic Ocean. Meet the continental shelf.

cards.headline: The shallow end
cards.body: A continental shelf is the broad, shallow, gently sloping underwater edge of a continent. It runs from the shore out to a sudden drop called the shelf break, usually at a depth of about 100 to 200 m. Compare that with Level 2's average ocean depth of about 3,700 m. If the ocean were a swimming pool, the shelves would be the shallow end.

cards.headline: Flat, flat, flat, then down
cards.body: The shelf is astonishingly flat. It tilts seaward by only about 0.1°, a drop of under 2 m for every kilometer. Walk a kilometer out along it and you'd descend less than the height of a doorway. Then comes the shelf break, and beyond it the much steeper continental slope drops toward the deep ocean floor. Widths vary a lot: narrow or almost absent along some coasts, enormous off Siberia.

cards.fact: Continental shelves cover only about 8% of the ocean's area.
cards.context: But they're some of its richest real estate. Level 8 showed there's rarely enough light for photosynthesis below about 200 m. Shelf water is shallow enough for sunlight to reach through it, and rivers wash in nutrients, so shelves support abundant sea life and rich fish populations. Small footprint, big menu.

title: Mid-Ocean Ridges
objective: After this level you can explain the longest mountain range on Earth.
summary: The mid-ocean ridge winds about 65,000 km around the globe, about 90% underwater: a chain of volcanoes where plates part and magma builds new sea floor. Marie Tharp found its central valley in 1952.

cards.headline: In 1952, Marie Tharp found a valley splitting an undersea mountain range.
cards.body: At Columbia University's Lamont lab, she was turning echo soundings of the Atlantic floor into profiles. Down the middle of an undersea mountain range, the profiles kept showing the same V-shaped notch. What could split a mountain range down the middle?

cards.headline: The longest mountain range on Earth
cards.body: Tharp was looking at one stretch of the mid-ocean ridge. It winds about 65,000 km around the globe, like the stitches on a baseball, which makes it the longest mountain range on Earth. And about 90% of it lies under the ocean. Earth's longest mountain range, and you've probably never seen it.

cards.headline: A mountain range that builds sea floor
cards.body: The ridge is the largest single volcanic feature on Earth: thousands of volcanoes and volcanic ridge segments that erupt from time to time. It rises from sea floor about 5 km deep to crests about 2.6 km below the surface. Along it, plates push apart and magma rises to fill the gap, building brand-new sea floor. The ridge isn't just scenery. It's a factory.

mascot.line: Dismissed as girl talk, confirmed by earthquakes. Trust the data, and the person who plotted it.

cards.headline: "Girl talk"
cards.body: Tharp's colleague Bruce Heezen at first dismissed her valley as "girl talk". By 1953 he was convinced: the locations of earthquakes turned out to line up inside it. The valley was real, and it ran right along the seam where the plates push apart. Tharp had found where the sea floor is made.

title: Trenches
objective: After this level you can describe the Mariana Trench and other deep trenches.
summary: Trenches form where an older, denser plate is pushed under another. The Mariana Trench, about 2,550 km long, holds Challenger Deep, where water adds more than 1,000 atmospheres.

cards.headline: Drop Mount Everest into the Mariana Trench and it disappears.
cards.body: Everest stands about 8,849 m tall. Set it on the floor of Challenger Deep, about 10,935 m down, and its peak would still be about 2 km underwater. Level 2 shrank this spot to a scratch on a desk globe. Up close, it's a canyon that swallows mountains.

cards.headline: Where the sea floor goes back down
cards.body: Trenches form where two plates converge. The older, denser plate is pushed down beneath the lighter one and plunges into the mantle, and the sea floor above the bend becomes a long, narrow, very deep trench. Most trenches are in the Pacific. If Level 13's ridges are where plates push apart to build sea floor, trenches are where sea floor heads back down into Earth.

cards.headline: The Mariana and its rivals
cards.body: The Mariana Trench is a crescent about 2,550 km long and only about 69 km wide on average: long and skinny, like a scratch from a giant fingernail. It holds Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in the ocean. But it has company. The Tonga, Kuril-Kamchatka, Philippine and Kermadec Trenches all plunge deeper than 10,000 m too.

mascot.line: More than a thousand atmospheres. I'd pack a very sturdy foam cup.

cards.headline: The deepest squeeze
cards.body: Remember Level 9's rule: about one extra atmosphere of pressure for every 10 m of seawater. Now run it at Challenger Deep, about 10,935 m below the surface. The water there adds more than 1,000 atmospheres. It's the deepest spot in the ocean, so it's also the heaviest stack of water on the planet.

title: Underwater Volcanoes
objective: After this level you can explain seamounts and volcanic islands.
summary: Seamounts are underwater mountains at least 1,000 m tall, mostly extinct volcanoes. One that grows tall enough becomes an island, like Surtsey in 1963; guyots are old islands planed flat and sunk.

cards.headline: In November 1963, a brand-new island rose out of the Atlantic.
cards.body: Off Iceland's south coast, an eruption that began on the sea floor, about 130 m down, broke through the waves. The new island was named Surtsey. Before it was an island, it was an underwater volcano. The sea floor has plenty of those.

cards.headline: A hundred thousand hidden peaks
cards.body: An underwater mountain with steep sides that rises at least 1,000 m above the surrounding sea floor is a seamount. Most are extinct volcanoes. Scientists estimate there are more than 100,000 of them, and less than one-tenth of a percent have been explored. Put another way: for every thousand seamounts, fewer than one has had a proper visit.

cards.headline: When a volcano breaks the surface
cards.body: Surtsey shows how a volcanic island is born: an eruption on the sea floor keeps building until the volcano pokes above the waves. Its eruptions lasted about three and a half years. Then the sea started pushing back. By 2008, waves had worn away almost half of its area. Building an island takes years; the ocean never stops sanding it down.

mascot.line: A flat-topped mountain a kilometer underwater is a clue. Something once flattened it at the surface.

cards.headline: Islands that sank
cards.body: Some seamounts have oddly flat tops. These guyots began as volcanic islands near the crests of mid-ocean ridges, where waves planed their summits flat. As the sea floor moved away from the ridge, it sank and carried them down; most of their summits now lie 1,000 to 2,000 m deep. A guyot is a drowned island still wearing the waves' haircut.

title: Hydrothermal Vents
objective: After this level you can describe hot springs on the sea floor.
summary: Seawater seeps into cracks near spreading ridges, is heated by magma and gushes back out at up to about 400°C, kept liquid by pressure. Its minerals build black-smoker chimneys.

cards.headline: In 1977, explorers found hot springs on the floor of the Pacific.
cards.body: On a spreading ridge near the Galápagos Islands, warm, chemical-rich water was flowing out of the sea floor, and it was surrounded by life nobody expected. The life is a story for a later level. First: how does a hot spring work at the bottom of a cold, dark ocean?

cards.headline: Plumbing made of rock
cards.body: A hydrothermal vent is a loop. Seawater seeps down through cracks in the ocean crust, gets heated by magma below, and rises back out as a hot spring. Most vents sit along the mid-ocean ridges, which makes sense after Level 13: that's where plates push apart and magma rises. The ocean pours in cold and comes back out hot.

cards.fact: Vent water can reach about 400°C and still not boil.
cards.context: That's four times the 100°C at which water boils at sea level. The trick is pressure. Remember Level 9: every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere, and the ridge crests where most vents sit lie about 2.6 km down. Squeezed that hard, the water stays liquid. Your kettle would be jealous.

mascot.line: A chimney that builds itself out of its own smoke. The sea floor has a flair for the dramatic.

cards.headline: Black smokers
cards.body: When that hot fluid meets near-freezing seawater, the minerals dissolved in it solidify. Black iron sulfide particles pour out like smoke, and the minerals pile up into chimneys that can grow tens of meters tall. Level 5 said vents help salt the sea. At a black smoker, you can watch some of that cargo drop out on arrival.

title: Sea-Floor Mud
objective: After this level you can explain what the ocean floor is covered with.
summary: Marine snow, organic bits sinking from above, piles up as ooze over about three-quarters of the deep floor, only about 6 m per million years. Sediment buries old hills to make flat abyssal plains.

cards.headline: It snows at the bottom of the ocean, all year round.
cards.body: No clouds, no cold front, and the flakes never melt. They drift down from the waters far above and take weeks to arrive. What is this snow, and what happens when it lands?

cards.headline: What's in a flake
cards.body: Marine snow is a slow shower of material from the upper ocean: bits of dead plants and animals and fecal matter, plus sand, soot and dust. Flakes can be several centimeters across. It's less a snowstorm than a very long fall of crumbs.

cards.headline: Ooze
cards.body: Whatever isn't eaten on the way piles up on the floor as ooze. Ooze and other slow-settling deep-sea sediments blanket about three-quarters of the deep ocean floor. Mud counts as ooze when more than 30% of it is the tiny shells and skeletons of microscopic sea life, made of calcium carbonate or silica. With less, it's called deep-sea clay or red clay.

cards.fact: Deep-sea ooze builds up by only about 6 m every million years.
cards.context: That's about half a millimeter in 80 years, a whole human lifetime. So each centimeter of ooze holds well over a thousand years of falling snow. The sea floor keeps a diary, one crumb at a time.

cards.headline: Tucked under a blanket
cards.body: Pile sediment up long enough and it buries the landscape. Abyssal plains, 3,000 to 6,000 m deep, are stretches of sea floor where sediment has filled in and smoothed an older, hilly floor. Their depth changes by only 10 to 100 cm per kilometer. The old hills are still down there, just tucked under the covers.

title: The Spreading Sea Floor
objective: After this level you can explain how the sea floor spreads and sinks.
summary: New sea floor forms at ridges, records Earth's flipping magnetic field in mirror-image stripes, sinks as it ages and returns into trenches. None is older than about 200 million years.

cards.headline: Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. Its sea floor is a youngster.
cards.body: The oldest known ocean floor is about 200 million years old: under 5% of Earth's age. Ocean-floor rocks are much younger than the rocks of the continents. So where did all the older sea floor go?

cards.headline: A conveyor belt of rock
cards.body: In 1960, geophysicist Harry Hess proposed an answer: seafloor spreading. New ocean floor forms at the mid-ocean ridges, where Level 13's magma rises. Old ocean floor sinks back down into the trenches of Level 14. The ocean basins are constantly recycled, which is also why Earth doesn't keep getting bigger. Ridges are where the conveyor belt comes out; trenches are where it goes back in.

mascot.line: A rock that remembers which way north pointed when it cooled. The sea floor keeps excellent records.

cards.headline: Stripes on the sea floor
cards.body: The evidence was written in magnetism. As lava cools into rock, grains of a magnetic mineral called magnetite lock in the direction of Earth's magnetic field, and that field has flipped many times. So the ocean floor carries stripes of alternating magnetic direction, running parallel to the ridge and matching on both sides of it. New rock forms in the middle and moves off both ways, like a barcode printed twice in mirror image.

cards.headline: Older, deeper, gone
cards.body: Walk away from a ridge and the floor gets older: youngest at the crest, older farther out. Level 15's guyots showed it sinks as it travels, too. Very little ocean floor is older than 150 million years, and the oldest known, about 200 million years old, lies in the far western Pacific. After that, it's back down a trench.

title: Tsunamis
objective: After this level you can explain how tsunamis cross whole oceans.
summary: A tsunami moves the whole water column, and deep water is its fast lane: over 800 km/h, crossing oceans in under a day. Pressure recorders on the sea floor can feel one just 1 cm high.

cards.headline: A tsunami from Alaska's Aleutian Islands can reach Hawaii in about five hours.
cards.body: Between them lies open Pacific. How does a wave cross that much ocean in an afternoon? And how would anyone spot one out in the middle of the sea?

cards.headline: The whole ocean moves
cards.body: Wind waves stir only the top layer of the ocean. A tsunami is different: it moves the entire water column, from the surface all the way down to the sea floor. Trenches like Level 14's can set them off: subduction-zone earthquakes caused the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and the 2011 Tohoku tsunami in Japan. A wind wave wrinkles the ocean's skin. A tsunami moves the whole body.

cards.headline: Deep water is the fast lane
cards.body: A tsunami's speed depends on the depth of the water: the deeper, the faster. Over the deep ocean it can move as fast as a jet plane, over 800 km/h, and cross an entire ocean in less than a day. And from Level 2, the open ocean averages about 3,700 m deep. For a tsunami, the middle of the ocean is an express lane.

mascot.line: One centimeter, felt through six kilometers of water. Now that's what I call paying attention.

cards.headline: Listening on the sea floor
cards.body: So how do you catch one mid-ocean? NOAA's DART stations put a pressure recorder on the sea floor. Remember Level 9: pressure comes from the water above you, about one atmosphere per 10 m. A tsunami moves the whole water column, so as it passes, the water overhead changes, and the recorder feels it. It can detect a tsunami as small as 1 cm in 6,000 m of water.

cards.headline: In 2008, NASA pulled the plug on the ocean.

cards.headline: Minus 6,000 m: only the trenches

title: How Waves Form
objective: After this level you can explain how wind makes waves.
summary: Wind makes waves; their size needs wind speed, time and fetch together. The water only circles, while the energy travels, and swell can cross an ocean.

cards.headline: A wave reaching Alaska can be born in a storm near Antarctica.
cards.body: In 1963, oceanographer Walter Munk and his team followed waves across the entire Pacific, from New Zealand to Alaska. We'll get to what they found. First, a smaller mystery: how does a breeze turn flat water into a wave at all?

cards.headline: Wind's three ingredients
cards.body: Most ocean waves start with wind rubbing on the water's surface. How big they grow takes three things: how fast the wind blows, how long it keeps blowing, and its fetch, the distance it travels over water in one direction. Large waves need all three at once. A fierce gust for a few minutes won't do it, and neither will a long gale over a short stretch of water. Your bathtub, sadly, has no fetch.
cards.callout: Big waves = strong wind + long time + long fetch

mascot.line: So a wave is more like a rumor than a river: the news travels, the water stays put.

cards.headline: The water stays home
cards.body: Here's the surprise: a wave carries energy, not water. As it passes, the water near the surface just turns in a circle about as wide as the wave is tall. The circles shrink with depth, and below about half a wavelength the water doesn't feel the wave at all. A rubber duck out at sea rides up, forward, down and back. The wave moves on. The duck stays home.

cards.fact: Munk's waves crossed the Pacific and lost very little energy.
cards.context: Waves that leave the wind that made them are called swell. Swell has smoother crests than wind waves and can run for thousands of miles. Munk's team tracked swell from Antarctic storms more than 16,000 km, and it arrived with very little energy lost. That clean surf on a calm day may have started in a storm an ocean away.

title: Why Waves Break
objective: After this level you can explain why waves break near the shore.
summary: In shallow water a wave drags on the bottom, slows, bunches up and grows taller. Its crest outruns its base and topples, where the water is about 1.3 times its height deep.

cards.headline: A wave can cross an ocean, then fall over in the last few meters.
cards.body: Level 21's swell can run thousands of miles without a stumble. Then it reaches the beach and collapses into foam. Nothing hit it. The sea floor simply came up to meet it.

cards.headline: The wave feels the floor
cards.body: Remember Level 21's circles of moving water, fading out about half a wavelength down? Once the sea gets shallower than that, the circles scrape the bottom and flatten. The wave slows. The waves behind catch up, so they bunch closer together, and the same energy squeezed into less room makes each wave taller. Near the beach, waves hit a traffic jam and pile up.

mascot.line: So every surfer is riding a wave that's tripping over its own feet. Gracefully, mind you.

cards.headline: The top outruns the bottom
cards.body: Friction holds back the bottom of the wave, but the crest keeps its speed. The front grows steeper and steeper until the crest is racing ahead with no water underneath it, and it topples forward. That's a breaker. As a rule of thumb, it happens where the water is about 1.3 times as deep as the wave is tall: a 1 m wave breaks in water about 1.3 m deep.

cards.fact: A wave breaks once it's taller than about a seventh of its length.
cards.context: That's the steepness limit, and a wave heading into shallow water gets pushed toward it from both sides: its length shrinks while its height grows. So breaking isn't bad luck. Every wave that runs out of deep water is on course for the same fall.

title: Rogue Waves
objective: After this level you can explain giant rogue waves.
summary: A rogue wave is more than twice the size of the waves around it. The Draupner wave, 25.6 m high on January 1, 1995, proved sailors' stories true.

cards.headline: For centuries, sailors described walls of water. Scientists doubted them.
cards.body: Then, on New Year's Day 1995, a laser on a gas platform in the North Sea measured one. The sailors had been right all along.

cards.headline: Big for the neighborhood
cards.body: A rogue wave isn't simply a big wave in a big storm. NOAA defines it by comparison: more than twice the size of the waves around it. Rogues are very unpredictable, often charge in from a different direction than the wind and the other waves, and tend to look like walls of water, steep-sided with unusually deep troughs. It's not just the size of the wave. It's the size of the surprise.

mascot.line: Twice as tall as the big waves around it. Sailors had every right to exaggerate, and it turns out they did not.

cards.fact: The Draupner wave stood 25.6 m high.
cards.context: Around the platform that day, the significant wave height (roughly the average of the highest third of waves) was almost 12 m. Draupner was more than twice that: a rogue by definition, caught by an instrument instead of a shaken sailor. The measurement confirmed that giant rogue waves are real.

cards.headline: When waves add up
cards.body: So where do rogues come from? Swells from different storms travel at different speeds and in different directions. Now and then their crests line up and reinforce each other, stacking into a towering wave that soon disappears. Rogues also form where storm waves run into a current flowing the other way, such as the Gulf Stream or the Agulhas Current, and those tend to last longer. Ordinary waves plus bad timing: one extraordinary wave.

title: Tides
objective: After this level you can explain how the Moon pulls the tides.
summary: The Moon raises two ocean bulges, so most coasts get two high tides a day. Tides run on 24 h 50 min lunar days, so they come about 50 minutes later each day.

cards.headline: High tide is late. Every single day.
cards.body: Check a tide table for a week. Each day, high tide shows up about 50 minutes later than the day before. The sea isn't slacking. It's keeping an appointment with the Moon.

cards.headline: Two bulges, two tides
cards.body: The Moon's gravity pulls the ocean into two bulges: one on the side of Earth facing the Moon, and one on the side facing away. Earth turns through both, so most shorelines get two high tides and two low tides a day, with a little over 12 hours from one high tide to the next. The water isn't rushing to your beach. Your beach is being carried into a bulge.
cards.callout: Two bulges, so two high tides a day

cards.headline: Chasing the Moon
cards.body: Why the daily delay? While Earth spins, the Moon moves along its orbit in the same direction. So after one full turn, your beach has to turn a little farther to get back under the Moon. That catch-up takes 50 minutes, which makes a lunar day 24 hours and 50 minutes long. The tides keep lunar time, so on our clocks they slide about 50 minutes later every day.

title: Spring and Neap Tides
objective: After this level you can explain how the Sun and Moon combine to make bigger and smaller tides.
summary: The Sun's tidal pull is a little under half the Moon's. Lined up at new and full moon they make spring tides; at right angles, neap tides. Perigee brings king tides.

cards.headline: The Sun outweighs the Moon 27 million times. It still moves the tides less.
cards.body: It's a distant heavyweight, about 390 times farther away than the Moon. Still, twice a month the Sun joins in, and that's when the tides get big.

cards.fact: The Sun's tidal pull is a little less than half the Moon's.
cards.context: Distance wins over mass when it comes to tides. So the Sun doesn't make a separate set of tides of its own. Its smaller solar tide rides on the Moon's, making each lunar tide a bit bigger or a bit smaller. The Moon sings lead; the Sun sings backup.

cards.headline: Teamwork, twice a month
cards.body: Twice a month, at new moon and full moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up. Their pulls add together: higher high tides and lower low tides. These are spring tides, named for the tide springing forth, not for the season. About seven days later, at the quarter moons, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and partly cancel. Those are neap tides: the highs a little lower, the lows a little higher.
cards.callout: Lined up: spring tides. Right angles: neap tides.

cards.headline: King tides
cards.body: One more dial. Once a month the Moon comes closest to Earth, a point called perigee, and its tide-raising force is higher than usual. The exceptionally high tides people call king tides typically come at a new or full moon, and perigee can push them higher still. "King tide" is a popular name, not a scientific one. The water doesn't mind.

title: The Biggest Tides
objective: After this level you can describe the Bay of Fundy and other huge tides.
summary: The Bay of Fundy's tide can rise 16 m because the bay sloshes in about 13 hours, nearly in step with the tide. Coastline shape, not the Moon, sets the range.

cards.headline: Same Moon, same tides? Not in the Bay of Fundy.
cards.body: The Moon pulls on every coast on Earth. Yet in one Canadian bay, the tide climbs as high as a four-story building. What makes this bay so special?

cards.fact: The tide at the head of the Bay of Fundy can rise 16 m.
cards.context: That's about the height of a four-story building. NOAA points to Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia, in the Bay of Fundy, as the home of the highest tides in the world. The Moon over Fundy is the same Moon that pulls on every other coast, so the secret must be in the bay itself.

mascot.line: Timing beats strength. A tiny push at the right moment is how you win at swings, and at tides.

cards.headline: A bathtub the size of a bay
cards.body: Slosh the water in a bathtub and it rocks from end to end in a few seconds. The Bay of Fundy rocks too, but one trip from its mouth to its head and back takes about 13 hours. The Atlantic tide floods in every 12 hours and 25 minutes, almost in step, so each tide gives the rocking another push. It's like pushing a child on a swing: small pushes at the right moment send it higher and higher.

cards.headline: Shape turns up the volume
cards.body: Fundy's narrow shape magnifies the range even more. Geography matters on a bigger scale too: NOAA notes that in the far north, North America, Europe and Asia are pressed close together, squeezing the ocean and raising tidal ranges. The highest tides in the United States are near Anchorage, Alaska, averaging around 30 feet (about 9 m). The Moon sets the rhythm. The coastline sets the volume.

title: Life Between the Tides
objective: After this level you can describe the animals of the zone between high and low tide.
summary: The intertidal zone stacks into spray, high, middle and low bands. Each species lives where it can handle the mix of air, water, heat and waves.

cards.headline: Some rocky shores wear stripes.
cards.body: Walk out on the rocks at low tide and look back up the shore. The plants and animals sit in distinct horizontal layers, one above another, like shelves in a pantry. The tides drew most of the lines.

cards.headline: A home that floods on schedule
cards.body: The intertidal zone is the strip where the ocean meets the land, between high and low tide. Its middle floods and drains twice a day. Living here means surviving swings in moisture, temperature and saltiness, and taking a pounding from waves. The higher up the rock you live, the longer you spend in the air: the high zone is underwater only at high tide, so it's hotter and drier. Imagine a house that floods twice a day, then bakes in between.

cards.headline: Four floors of the shore
cards.body: From the top down: the spray zone is only splashed, except in extreme high tides and storms. The high zone, underwater only at high tide, is home to hardy barnacles, snails and limpets. The middle zone spends about equal time wet and dry; mussels, sea stars and anemones live here. The low zone is almost always underwater, uncovered only by the lowest spring tides, and it holds the greatest variety of life, because it suits creatures that can't take long in the air.

cards.headline: Who gets which floor
cards.body: Why such neat layers? Each species lives where it can handle the balance of air and water, and where predators and competitors for space and food let it. Barnacles can take long hours high and dry. Sea urchins stay down in the low zone, where the sea almost never leaves. Each stripe on the rock marks a line where the rules of survival change.

title: Tidal Power
objective: After this level you can explain how tides can make electricity.
summary: Tidal barrages like La Rance (1966) trap the tide and release it through turbines; stream turbines stand in fast currents. Tides are predictable, but barrages change estuaries.

cards.headline: In 1966, France dammed an estuary to catch the tide.
cards.body: The La Rance power station in Brittany turns the rise and fall of the sea into electricity, and it is still running today. How do you harvest water that only goes up and down?

cards.headline: A dam that breathes
cards.body: La Rance is a tidal barrage: a dam across a tidal basin. As the tide rises, its gates let the sea flood in. As the tide falls, the trapped water rushes back out through turbines. La Rance has 24 of them and 240 MW of capacity; South Korea's Sihwa Lake, at 254 MW, is now the largest. The catch: it only pays with a tidal range of at least 10 feet (about 3 m). Level 26's Bay of Fundy clears that bar easily.

cards.headline: Windmills underwater
cards.body: The other approach skips the dam. Tidal stream turbines stand in fast tidal currents, often around islands and coasts, and work like wind turbines: moving fluid turns the blades, the blades turn a rotor. But water is about 800 times denser than air, so these machines must be much sturdier and heavier. Picture a wind turbine built by someone expecting a very rough day.

mascot.line: A power plant that runs on the Moon and checks the calendar. Very punctual.

cards.fact: Unlike the wind, the tide keeps its schedule.
cards.context: Tides are predictable (Level 24 showed their Moon-driven timetable), which makes them a promising source of steady, reliable power. The cost falls on the estuary: a barrage can change the tide level behind it, make the water murkier and block fish from swimming in or out.

title: Storm Surges
objective: After this level you can explain storm surges.
summary: A storm surge is sea level lifted by a storm's winds and piled up by shallow coasts. Added to the tide, it becomes the storm tide. Katrina's reached 27.8 feet.

cards.headline: In 2005, the sea rose 27.8 feet at Pass Christian, Mississippi.
cards.body: That's about 8.5 m of seawater, the highest mark of Hurricane Katrina's storm surge. The wind did most of the lifting. How?

cards.headline: Wind piles up the sea
cards.body: A storm surge is the rise in sea level caused by the storm itself, mainly by its winds shoving water toward the shore. Out in deep water, the pushed water can circulate down and away. Near the coast, the sea floor blocks it, so the water has nowhere to go but up and inland. A gently sloping shelf or a curved-in bay makes the surge bigger. Think of blowing across a bowl of soup: the soup climbs the far side.

cards.headline: Surge plus tide
cards.body: The surge doesn't replace the tide; it rides on top of it. Forecasters call the total the storm tide: surge plus the normal astronomical tide. So timing matters. A storm that strikes around a new or full moon lands on Level 25's spring tides, when the tides are already at their biggest, and the water climbs highest of all.

mascot.line: Worth remembering: in a hurricane, it's the water, not the wind, that you most need to get away from.

cards.fact: In a hurricane, the water is the greatest threat to life.

title: Surface Currents
objective: After this level you can explain how wind drives surface currents.
summary: Winds drag the sea's surface into currents, Earth's spin bends them, and together they make five great gyres that turn clockwise up north.

cards.headline: In 1992, a load of bath toys fell into the Pacific. Then they went sightseeing.
cards.body: In January 1992 a cargo ship lost thousands of plastic bath toys in the North Pacific. Nobody steered them, yet that November beachcombers started finding them in Alaska. How did a flotilla of plastic ducks know where to go?

cards.headline: The wind drags the sea along
cards.body: Winds drive the currents at and near the ocean's surface. As the wind blows, it drags the top layer of water along with it by friction, the same grip that lets you slide a tablecloth by pushing your palm across it. Oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer and NOAA's James Ingraham used the toys' landings to test a computer model that works out surface currents from the winds. The ducks weren't navigating. They were hitchhiking.

mascot.line: Imagine pushing a boat and having the whole planet quietly nudge it sideways. Rude, but reliable.

cards.headline: Earth's spin bends the path
cards.body: Polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen spotted something odd: sea ice didn't drift straight downwind. It veered 20 to 40 degrees to the right, and he blamed Earth's rotation. He was right. Because the planet spins, moving air and water get deflected: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern. It's called the Coriolis effect, after the mathematician Gaspard Gustave de Coriolis.

cards.headline: Gyres: the ocean's giant loops
cards.body: Put steady winds and that sideways nudge together over a whole ocean, and the currents bend into gyres: huge rotating systems of currents, thousands of kilometers across. There are five major ones, in the North and South Pacific, the North and South Atlantic and the Indian Ocean. North of the equator they turn clockwise; south of it, counterclockwise. Right up north, left down south: the same rule that bent Nansen's ice.

title: The Gulf Stream
objective: After this level you can explain the Gulf Stream and how it warms Europe.
summary: The Gulf Stream is a warm river in the Atlantic that Franklin charted. It carries heat north, and westerly winds bring that warmth to Europe.

cards.headline: In the 1760s, mail ships took up to two weeks longer to sail west than east.
cards.body: Same ocean, similar distance, very different trip. Benjamin Franklin wanted to know why. The answer turned out to be a river hidden in the Atlantic.

cards.headline: The whalers already knew
cards.body: In 1768 Franklin, then deputy postmaster general for the colonies, asked his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket captain and former whaler. Whalers knew of a warm, strong current and used it, Folger explained; the mail captains didn't, and sailed right against it. Folger sketched it, Franklin printed a chart naming the Gulph Stream, and it went to the mail ships in 1769 or 1770. The captains seem to have ignored it. Some people just won't ask for directions.

cards.headline: A river inside the ocean
cards.body: The Gulf Stream is a warm current that moves north along the coast of Florida, turns east off North Carolina and flows northeast across the Atlantic. It averages about 6.4 km/h, a brisk walking pace, which is a lot for a whole river of seawater. And it is a river: it carries more water than all the world's rivers combined.
cards.callout: Warm · about 6.4 km/h · more water than every river on Earth

cards.headline: Europe's hot-water bottle
cards.body: The Gulf Stream is the Atlantic's main conveyor of heat from south to north. In the cold far north, its warm water heats the air above it, and prevailing westerly winds carry that warmth and moisture onto northwestern Europe. The result: Bergen, Norway, gets milder winters than New York, which lies much further south. Same ocean, opposite side of the radiator.

title: The Great Ocean Conveyor
objective: After this level you can explain the slow circulation of the deep ocean.
summary: Cold, salty water sinks in the far North Atlantic and drives a slow conveyor round the globe: about 1,000 years a lap. The IPCC expects it to weaken.

cards.headline: One cubic meter of seawater takes about 1,000 years to lap the ocean.
cards.body: No wind pushes it. The engine is something you met in Level 6: cold, salty water is heavy, and heavy water sinks.

cards.headline: Where the ocean sinks
cards.body: In the far North Atlantic, the water is chilled by Arctic air. When sea ice forms, the salt doesn't freeze; it's left behind in the water around the ice. Now that water is cold and extra salty, so it's dense, and it sinks toward the bottom. Surface water moves in to replace it, and that creates a current. Freezing a bit of sea helps power a planet-sized pump.

cards.headline: The slowest current on Earth
cards.body: This deep, slow circulation is called thermohaline circulation: thermo for temperature, haline for salt, because density differences from both drive it. The global conveyor belt it forms moves at a few centimeters per second. At that crawl, any given cubic meter of water takes about 1,000 years to complete the journey. Water sinking this year won't finish the loop for about ten centuries.
cards.callout: Driven by heat and salt · about 1,000 years per lap

mascot.line: Scientists choose these words carefully, and so should we: 'very likely weaker' is not the same as 'switched off'.

cards.headline: Will the conveyor slow?
cards.body: The Atlantic part of the conveyor, the AMOC, carries warm water from the tropics north. Warming seas and extra fresh water from rain and melting ice make the surface water lighter, so less of it sinks. The IPCC (2021) says the AMOC will very likely weaken this century, with low confidence in how much, and medium confidence that it will not collapse abruptly before 2100.

title: El Niño
objective: After this level you can explain El Niño and its effects on weather.
summary: When the Pacific's trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east, upwelling fades, and the weather shifts from the US to the whole planet's temperature.

cards.headline: Fishermen in South America named a warm-water mystery after Christmas.
cards.body: Every few years, around the end of the year, their coastal sea turned warmer and the fish catches fell. They called it El Niño, Spanish for little boy, after the Christmas holiday. Today we know the whole planet feels it.

cards.headline: A normal year: the wind piles up warm water
cards.body: Normally, trade winds blow west along the equator, pushing warm surface water from South America toward Asia. Off South America, cold, nutrient-rich water rises from the depths to replace it. That rising water, called upwelling, feeds a rich coastal sea. Think of it as the wind sweeping the warm top layer to one side of the Pacific's bathtub.

cards.headline: El Niño: the wind eases off
cards.body: In an El Niño, the trade winds across the tropical Pacific are weaker than usual, and the central and eastern tropical Pacific runs warmer than average. Off South America, upwelling weakens or stops, so fewer phytoplankton grow, which hits the fish and everything that eats fish. La Niña is the opposite phase. The swings come every 2 to 7 years on average, and an episode typically lasts 9 to 12 months.

mascot.line: So a fisherman's Christmas puzzle turned out to be a clue to the whole world's weather. Nice work, fishermen.

cards.headline: One ocean, the whole world's weather
cards.body: Because the Pacific is so big, its mood travels. During El Niño, the northern US and Canada tend to be drier and warmer than usual, while the US Gulf Coast and Southeast are wetter, with more flooding. It even nudges the planet's temperature: the warmest year of a decade tends to be an El Niño year. A warm patch of one ocean can reset the thermostat for everyone.

title: Warm Seas, Big Storms
objective: After this level you can explain how warm seas fuel hurricanes.
summary: Hurricanes run on seawater of at least 26.5°C: evaporation and condensation turn heat into wind. They weaken over land and leave cooler sea behind.

cards.headline: A hurricane is a heat engine, and warm seawater is its fuel.
cards.body: Cut off the warm water and the monster starves. That's why hurricanes are born over tropical and subtropical seas, and why they fade once they hit land.

cards.fact: A hurricane needs seawater of at least 26.5°C, reaching down about 50 m.
cards.context: A warm film on top isn't enough: the warmth has to run deep. That's a tank of fuel, not a puddle, and only warm seas can fill it.

cards.headline: How warm water becomes wind
cards.body: Warm water evaporates, making warm, moist air that rises into the storm. As it rises it cools, and the vapor condenses into clouds, releasing even more heat that powers the storm. Once a hurricane hits land, it runs out of warm, moist air and its winds weaken; over cold water it loses its fuel too. Starve the engine and it stalls.

cards.headline: The storm cools the sea behind it
cards.body: Remember Level 6: warm water sits on top of a much colder layer, with the thermocline between. A hurricane's winds churn up that cooler water from below, so the sea it leaves behind can be several degrees Celsius cooler. The storm literally burns through its own fuel as it goes, leaving a cold wake.

cards.headline: Warmer world, stronger storms
cards.body: The IPCC (2021) finds a likely rise in the share of major hurricanes worldwide over the last four decades, and projects a larger share of the most intense storms with more warming. Whether the total number of storms is changing is far less clear: the IPCC has low confidence in long-term trends in their count.

title: The Ocean's Heat
objective: After this level you can explain how the ocean stores heat.
summary: A thin skin of ocean holds as much heat as the whole atmosphere. The ocean has soaked up about 91% of the extra heat, and marine heatwaves have doubled.

cards.headline: The top few meters of the ocean hold as much heat as Earth's entire atmosphere.
cards.body: Picture all the air above you, right up to space. A thin skin of seawater stores the same amount of heat. That makes the ocean the planet's biggest heat battery.

cards.headline: Slow to warm, slow to cool
cards.body: Water can absorb a lot of heat without its temperature rising much, and it is slower to heat up and cool down than air or land. You've felt this at the beach: at noon the sand scorches your feet while the sea still feels cool. The water has taken in just as much sunshine. It simply hides it better.

cards.fact: The ocean has taken up about 91% of the extra heat trapped in the climate system.
cards.context: That's the IPCC's 2021 figure, and the atmosphere, where we live, got only about 1%. It's virtually certain the upper ocean, down to 700 m, has warmed since the 1970s, and extremely likely that people are the main driver. The warming you feel in the air is the small change; the sea is carrying most of the bill.

cards.headline: Heatwaves under the waves
cards.body: Store that much heat and the sea gets hot spells of its own. Marine heatwaves are spells of persistent, unusually warm sea temperatures, and the IPCC reports with high confidence that they have roughly doubled in frequency since the 1980s. The battery isn't just big. It's charging.

title: The Ocean and Carbon
objective: After this level you can explain how the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide.
summary: The ocean takes up about 30% of released CO2: it dissolves best in cold water and plankton carry some deep. The cost is a more acidic sea.

cards.headline: About 30% of the carbon dioxide released into the air ends up in the sea.
cards.body: Every exhaust pipe and chimney sends up carbon dioxide, and nearly a third of it gets pulled down into the ocean. How does a sea swallow a gas, and what does it cost?

cards.headline: Fizz in reverse
cards.body: Carbon dioxide dissolves into seawater at the surface, like the fizz in a soda, only running the other way: in, not out. Colder water can hold more of it than warmer water, which is also why a cold soda stays fizzier than a warm one. Once dissolved, the carbon dioxide reacts with the water to form carbonic acid.

cards.headline: Plankton pump it down
cards.body: Remember Level 1's plankton, making about half of Earth's oxygen? The same photosynthesis takes up carbon dioxide. That carbon passes up the food web, and a portion sinks toward the deep sea, where it can stay for hundreds to thousands of years. Scientists call it the biological carbon pump. Tiny drifters, very long storage.

cards.headline: The cost: a more acidic sea
cards.body: All that carbonic acid is changing seawater. Ocean acidification is a long-term drop in the ocean's pH caused mainly by taking up carbon dioxide, and the IPCC says it's virtually certain human emissions are the main driver. It leaves fewer carbonate ions, the building blocks of shells, so oysters, clams, sea urchins and corals struggle. Imagine building a house while someone keeps taking bricks off your pile.

title: Rising Seas
objective: After this level you can explain why sea level is rising.
summary: Seas have risen about 21 to 24 cm since 1880 as warming water expands and land ice melts. The rise is speeding up, and the IPCC expects more.

cards.headline: Global sea level has risen about 21–24 cm since 1880.
cards.body: That's a bit more than the length of a new pencil, added to every coastline on Earth. And the rise is speeding up. So where is all that extra water coming from?

cards.headline: Two taps are running
cards.body: Sea level rises for two main reasons. First, seawater expands as it warms, and Level 36 showed the ocean has taken up about 91% of the extra heat. Second, glaciers and ice sheets on land are melting and adding water. From 1971 to 2018, the IPCC found expansion caused about 50% of the rise, glaciers about 22% and ice sheets about 20%. Same ocean, just puffed up and topped up.

cards.headline: Not a trickle any more
cards.body: The rise isn't steady. The IPCC measured about 1.3 mm a year from 1901 to 1971, and about 3.7 mm a year from 2006 to 2018: nearly three times as fast. Human influence was very likely the main driver since at least 1971. A millimeter sounds tiny, but a tap that keeps speeding up eventually fills the bath.

mascot.line: Notice the ranges. The future sea isn't one number, and the choices people make move it.

cards.headline: What the IPCC expects
cards.body: It depends on us. By 2100, the IPCC's likely rise is 0.28–0.55 m with very low emissions and 0.63–1.01 m with very high emissions, compared with 1995–2014. Rises approaching 2 m can't be ruled out, because ice-sheet behavior is deeply uncertain, and sea level is committed to keep rising for centuries.

title: Garbage Patches
objective: After this level you can explain how plastic gathers in ocean gyres.
summary: Gyres draw floating debris into their calm centers. The resulting patches are mostly microplastics, like pepper in soup, and very hard to clean.

cards.headline: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch isn't an island of trash. It's more like soup.
cards.body: People picture a floating landfill you could walk across. The real thing is stranger and harder to fix, and it sits where it does because of the gyres you met in Level 31.

cards.headline: Where the currents dump it
cards.body: Garbage patches are large areas of ocean where litter, fishing gear and other debris collect, and gyres make them. A gyre's circling currents draw floating debris into its calm, stable center. The best-known patch lies in the North Pacific gyre, between Hawaii and California. Captain Charles Moore came upon it in 1997, sailing home from a yacht race, and saw plastic all around his boat.

cards.headline: Pepper, not islands
cards.body: Most of a garbage patch is microplastics: plastic pieces smaller than 5 mm, along with bigger junk like abandoned fishing nets. NOAA likens it to pepper flakes swirling in a soup, spread from the surface all the way to the ocean floor. You couldn't walk on it, and satellite images don't show it.

mascot.line: The good news hides in that sink picture: the tap is the part people can actually reach.

cards.headline: Why you can't just scoop it up
cards.body: Because the pieces are tiny, spread out and always moving with currents and wind, nobody can give a patch an exact size, and cleaning one up entirely may not be possible. NOAA says prevention is key: when a sink overflows, you turn off the tap before you mop the floor.

title: Checkpoint: Currents and Climate
objective: After this level you can explain how ocean currents shape climate.
summary: Follow one parcel of warm water: pushed by wind, carried north by the Gulf Stream, sunk into a 1,000-year conveyor. Currents spread Earth's heat.

cards.headline: Follow one parcel of warm water, and you'll travel the whole chapter.
cards.body: Its trip ties together the winds, the Gulf Stream and the slow deep sea. Along the way, you'll see why currents and climate are really one system.

cards.fact: Ocean currents carry warm water away from the equator and cold water from the poles, evening out Earth's heat.
cards.context: It's the planet's central heating, with pipes thousands of kilometers long. Every level in this chapter is part of that plumbing.

cards.headline: The trip
cards.body: Winds push our parcel along the surface into the Gulf Stream, which carries it north along Florida and then northeast across the Atlantic. In the cold far north it hands its heat to the air, and westerly winds carry that warmth to Europe. Now cold and salty, it sinks and joins the deep conveyor, where one lap takes about 1,000 years.

cards.headline: Heat, carbon and everything else
cards.body: The whole time, the ocean is doing climate's heavy lifting. It has taken up about 91% of the extra heat and about 30% of the carbon dioxide released into the air. Warm seas of at least 26.5°C fuel hurricanes, and the gyres gather our plastic into patches of microplastics. Currents and climate: one system.

title: Plankton
objective: After this level you can explain plankton as the base of the ocean food web.
summary: Plankton drift wherever the current takes them. Phytoplankton catch sunlight in the top of the sea and feed nearly everything else, from zooplankton to whales.

cards.headline: One of the ocean's biggest oxygen makers is too small to see.
cards.body: It's called Prochlorococcus, the smallest photosynthetic organism on Earth. NOAA says it makes up to 20% of the oxygen in our entire biosphere, more than all the tropical rainforests on land combined. It's plankton. Time to meet the drifters who run the sea.

cards.headline: Drifters, not swimmers
cards.body: Plankton isn't one kind of creature. It's more like a job description: anything carried along by tides and currents that can't swim well enough to fight them. The name comes from the Greek for drifter. Most plankton are microscopic, but the club also has some big, floppy members, like certain jellyfish. If the current says go, you go.

cards.headline: The plants and the grazers
cards.body: Scientists split plankton into two teams. Phytoplankton are the plants: like land plants, they use chlorophyll to catch sunlight and make food by photosynthesis. Zooplankton are the animals, and most of them eat phytoplankton. Then most zooplankton get eaten by something bigger. That's why NASA calls phytoplankton the foundation of the food web, feeding everything from zooplankton to multi-ton whales.

mascot.line: A meadow nobody can see, feeding almost everybody. Not bad for a bunch of drifters.

cards.headline: A meadow you can see from space
cards.body: Remember Level 8: below about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis. So the ocean's whole pasture grows in a thin sunlit top layer. It's a busy pasture. From Level 1, about half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean, mostly made by plankton. And when phytoplankton bloom, they can cover hundreds of square kilometers, easily visible in satellite images. A meadow you can see from orbit, made of things you can't see at all.

title: Kelp Forests
objective: After this level you can describe underwater kelp forests.
summary: Kelp are giant brown algae that race up to 60 cm a day toward the light. Their shallow forests shelter thousands of species, as long as otters keep the urchins in check.

cards.headline: This forest can grow 60 cm in a day, and it isn't made of plants.
cards.body: Along much of the west coast of North America, forests rise from the sea floor toward the light. Their "trees" are giant kelp. So what are they, and why do they grow so fast?

cards.headline: Built like a tree, but not a tree
cards.body: Kelp are large brown algae, not plants, and they like cool, nutrient-rich coastal water. Instead of roots, a kelp grips the rock with a root-like holdfast. Instead of a trunk, it has flexible stems called stipes, with leaf-like blades reaching for the sunlight. Many kelp also carry gas-filled bladders that float the blades upward. Picture a tree with an anchor for roots and water wings on its leaves.

cards.fact: Giant kelp can grow up to 2 feet (about 60 cm) in a single day.
cards.context: That makes it one of the fastest-growing organisms on Earth. It needs the speed. Like the phytoplankton in Level 41, kelp runs on sunlight, so kelp forests rarely grow deeper than about 15 to 40 m. The whole forest is a race to the surface.

mascot.line: Sometimes a forest's best friend is whoever eats the things that eat it.

cards.headline: A forest with a weak spot
cards.body: Once the fronds reach the top, they spread into a floating canopy that shades the water below. Beneath it live thousands of species of fish, invertebrates and marine mammals: more variety than almost any other ocean community. The weak spot is sea urchins, which graze on kelp. Predators like sea otters and sea stars keep urchins in check. When urchins surge, they can strip whole forests, leaving bare rock called urchin barrens.

title: Coral Reefs
objective: After this level you can explain why coral reefs hold so much life.
summary: Reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean but house nearly a quarter of its species. Polyps build the city, and algae in their tissues feed it with sunlight.

cards.headline: Less than 1% of the ocean. Nearly a quarter of its species.
cards.body: Coral reefs are specks on a map of the sea, yet they are packed like nowhere else. Why would so much life crowd into so little space? The answer is a building, a lodger and a lot of sunshine.

cards.headline: A city built by animals
cards.body: A reef is built by coral polyps, tiny soft animals that each lay down a hard limestone skeleton. Hundreds to thousands of them make one coral, and corals together make a reef full of ledges, holes and hideouts. Fish, crabs and sea turtles use it to feed, shelter and raise their young. NOAA calls reefs the rainforests of the sea. On a reef, the scenery is also the housing.

cards.headline: The lodger that pays the rent
cards.body: Living inside the coral's tissues are microscopic algae. The coral gives them shelter, plus the carbon dioxide and water they need for photosynthesis. In return, as much as 90% of the food the algae make passes to the coral. It's one of the best rental deals in nature: the tenant pays in food, and the landlord builds a whole city on it.
cards.callout: Coral: shelter · Algae: up to 90% of their food

cards.headline: Why reefs need clear, sunny water
cards.body: Here's the catch. The lodgers run on sunlight, so reef-building corals thrive in clear, warm, moving tropical water where light reaches their algae. Remember Level 8: light fades with depth, and below about 200 m there's too little for photosynthesis. Like the kelp of Level 42, which rarely grows deeper than about 15 to 40 m, reef builders are solar-powered. For them, murky water is a power cut.

title: Schools of Fish
objective: After this level you can explain why fish swim in schools.
summary: Fish school to dodge predators, find food and mates, and save energy. With no leader, each fish follows its neighbors by sight and by the pressure-sensing lateral line.

cards.headline: Thousands of fish, no leader, and they can all turn in under a second.
cards.body: Watch a school swerve and it looks rehearsed. Nobody is in charge. So why do fish crowd together, and how do they move as one?

cards.headline: Safety, food and company
cards.body: A reef offers hideouts and nurseries, as you saw in Level 43. A school is another answer to the same problem. Fish swim together to evade predators, to find good feeding areas, to find mates and to save energy. Out in open water, a fish's best hiding place is the crowd around it.

cards.fact: In a 2024 study, fish in schools used up to 79% less energy in rough water.
cards.context: Harvard zoologist Yangfan Zhang and colleagues put giant danios in turbulent water, swimming alone or in groups of eight. The schooling fish used up to 79% less energy than the loners. It's like cycling in a pack instead of alone into the wind.

mascot.line: No captain, no map, no meeting. Just thousands of fish each watching the one next door.

cards.headline: No leader, just neighbors
cards.body: Each fish keeps its place with its eyes and its lateral line, a row of cells along its body that feels pressure changes as neighbors move. It times its tail beats to follow the fish beside it, like dancers moving to the same beat. When a predator strikes, only a few fish may see it, but the alarm spreads, and in less than a second thousands move as one shape. In dark water, though, each fish can keep in step only with its closest neighbors.

title: Sea Turtles
objective: After this level you can describe sea turtles' long journeys.
summary: Hatchlings dash to sea and grow up among floating seaweed. Years later, females return to their home beach, likely by its magnetic signature. Leatherbacks cross the whole Pacific.

cards.headline: She left this beach as a hatchling. Years later, she comes back to lay her eggs.
cards.body: In between, she may cross an ocean. How does a turtle find one small beach on a planet where the ocean covers more than 70% of the surface?

cards.headline: The great escape
cards.body: It starts with a dash. Sea turtle hatchlings burst from the nest almost all at once, which helps them overwhelm the predators waiting on the sand. They find the sea by the beach's downward slope and the glint of moon and stars on the water. The survivors swim out to floating mats of sargassum seaweed, where they spend their early years hiding and growing. A floating nursery, far from shore.

cards.headline: Coming home
cards.body: Years later, female sea turtles return to nest on the very beaches where they hatched. How? Scientists think it's magnetism. Every stretch of coast has its own magnetic signature, a mix of the strength and angle of Earth's magnetic field. Hatchlings imprint on it and use it as adults to find the way back. Every beach has a magnetic address, and a turtle memorizes hers on the way out the door.

mascot.line: The world's biggest turtle, powered by jelly. Somebody tell the sandwich industry.

cards.fact: Leatherbacks cross the Pacific: nearly 7,000 miles, about 11,000 km.
cards.context: Western Pacific leatherbacks nest in Indonesia and feed off the Pacific coast of North America, a crossing that takes 10 to 12 months. The leatherback is the largest turtle in the world, and it fuels the trip on soft open-ocean prey such as jellyfish. Remember Level 41: jellyfish are drifters. A giant crossing an ocean on a diet of plankton.

title: Dolphins
objective: After this level you can describe how dolphins hunt and communicate.
summary: Light fades fast in the sea, but sound races through it. Dolphins read echoes to find prey, call each other by signature whistles and herd fish schools as a team.

cards.headline: In the sea, light fades fast. Sound doesn't.
cards.body: Remember Level 8: a few meters down the reds are gone, and below 1,000 m there's no sunlight at all. Dolphins solved the problem of a dim world by hunting and talking with sound.

cards.headline: A world built for sound
cards.body: Sound travels about 1,500 m per second in seawater, over four times faster than the roughly 340 m per second it manages in air. It also carries much farther in the sea. So underwater, your eyes are the weak sense and your ears are the strong one. The ocean is dim, but it is never quiet.

cards.headline: Seeing with echoes
cards.body: Dolphins use echolocation to fill in what they can't see. They send out sounds, focus them with the melon (that big rounded forehead) and read the echoes that bounce back. NOAA says a dolphin can interpret echolocation signals from about half a mile (roughly 800 m) away. It's a flashlight made of sound, and it works in the dark.

mascot.line: Imagine a name you can only whistle. Now imagine your mom whistling it across the whole bay.

cards.headline: Names and teamwork
cards.body: Sound is also how dolphins keep in touch. Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle, a call that works like a name. They hunt as a team, too. Remember the schools of Level 44? Bottlenose dolphins herd fish into tight groups, then take turns charging through to feed. They may even trap a school against a sandbar or seawall. The fish's crowd trick meets a crowd with a plan.

title: Seals and Sea Lions
objective: After this level you can tell seals from sea lions.
summary: Seals and sea lions are both pinnipeds. Sea lions have ear flaps, walk on their flippers and bark; seals have ear holes, wriggle on their bellies and are built for the water.

cards.headline: That "seal" balancing a ball at the aquarium show? Probably a sea lion.
cards.body: NOAA notes that sea lions are the ones more likely to star in marine shows. The two get mixed up all the time. A few quick clues and you never will again.

cards.headline: Flipper-footed
cards.body: Seals and sea lions belong to a group called pinnipeds, which means fin- or flipper-footed. Walruses are the third member. All of them are mammals that live in the ocean but can come on land for long stretches. They have a foot in each world, and each foot is a flipper.

mascot.line: Quick test: flaps and a bark? Sea lion. Holes and a wriggle? Seal. You're officially dangerous at aquariums.

cards.headline: Built for different worlds
cards.body: Why the difference? Seals are better adapted to life in the water than on land, and they are more streamlined swimmers than sea lions. Their rear flippers can't rotate forward, so on a beach they hump along like caterpillars. Sea lions trade some of that sleekness for agility on land. A seal on a beach isn't clumsy; it's just off duty.
