title: Seabirds
objective: After this level you can describe albatrosses, puffins and other seabirds.
summary: Albatrosses glide for hours without flapping and come ashore only to breed. Puffins fly underwater. And every seabird drinks the sea, thanks to salt glands above its eyes.

cards.headline: One seabird has been coming back to the same island since 1956.
cards.body: Her name is Wisdom, a Laysan albatross first banded on Midway Atoll in 1956. She is the world's oldest known wild bird, and she was still laying eggs in her 70s. How does a bird build a whole life on the open sea?

cards.headline: Flying without flapping
cards.body: The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird, more than 340 cm. Albatrosses use those long, narrow wings to stay aloft in windy weather for hours without flapping: they glide downwind toward the sea, then turn into the wind to climb back up. They come ashore only to breed, and a young albatross can spend 5 to 10 years at sea first. The wind does the work.

cards.headline: Flying underwater
cards.body: Puffins take the opposite approach. An Atlantic puffin "flies" underwater, using its wings as paddles and its webbed feet to steer, and can dive to about 200 feet (about 60 m). It can catch as many as 10 small fish in a row and carry them crosswise in its bill back to the nest. Somehow it keeps hold of the first fish while catching the tenth.

mascot.line: So when a gull looks like it has a runny nose, it is actually running a salt factory.

cards.headline: Drinking the sea
cards.body: Out at sea there's nothing to drink but seawater, and from Level 5 you know it's about 35 parts per thousand salt. Seabirds cope with a pair of salt glands above their eyes. The glands act like an extra set of kidneys, pulling surplus salt out of the blood. It drips from the nostrils as brine. Every seabird carries a tiny desalination plant, right between its eyes and its beak.

title: Sharks
objective: After this level you can explain why sharks matter to healthy seas.
summary: Sharks keep prey in balance and, just by being around, can protect seagrass meadows. Yet oceanic sharks and rays have fallen by 71% since 1970.

cards.headline: In one Australian bay, sharks protect seagrass without eating a single blade.
cards.body: It sounds like a riddle. The answer explains why a sea with sharks is healthier than a sea without them.

cards.headline: The ocean's quality control
cards.body: Sharks are apex predators, at the top of the ocean food web. They help keep ecosystems in balance by preying on sick, weak or overabundant animals, so no single species takes over. That indirectly protects habitats like the coral reefs of Level 43, which pack nearly a quarter of ocean species into less than 1% of the ocean. Sharks aren't the villains of the reef; they're its referees.

mascot.line: Think of it as a lifeguard who never leaves the chair, and still keeps everyone off the lawn.

cards.headline: The fear factor
cards.body: Now the riddle. In Shark Bay, Western Australia, dugongs and green turtles graze on seagrass. Tiger sharks change when, where and how they graze: with sharks around, the grazers crowd to the safer edges of the seagrass banks. Researchers think the seagrass beds might be very different without the sharks. A predator can protect a meadow just by being there.

cards.fact: Oceanic sharks and rays have declined by 71% since 1970.
cards.context: That's the finding of a 2021 study in Nature, which blamed an 18-fold rise in relative fishing pressure. Take the referees out of the game and the balance they keep starts to slip, all the way down the food web.

title: Zones of the Deep
objective: After this level you can name the ocean's depth zones.
summary: Sunlight zone to 200 m, twilight to 1,000 m, then the midnight zone (to 4,000 m), the abyss (to 6,000 m) and the hadal zone in the trenches.

cards.headline: Take an elevator down the ocean, and only the first stop has daylight.
cards.body: Oceanographers split the sea into zones stacked like floors, and they sort them by one thing: how much sunlight gets in. Press the down button. Five stops, one sunny.

cards.headline: Sunlight, then twilight
cards.body: First stop: the sunlight zone, the top 200 m. Remember Level 8: below about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis. So the next stop, from 200 to 1,000 m, is the twilight zone, where light fades fast into a dim blue dusk that never turns to day. At 1,000 m, even that is gone.

cards.fact: The midnight zone holds about 70% of all the seawater on Earth.
cards.context: It runs from 1,000 to 4,000 m, in total darkness at a steady 4°C, which makes it the largest single habitat on the planet. The only light down here is the kind living things make themselves. The biggest home on Earth has never had a sunrise.

mascot.line: The deeper the floor, the spookier the name. I respect the commitment.

cards.headline: The abyss and the hadal zone
cards.body: Below 4,000 m comes the abyss, down to 6,000 m. Deeper still is the hadal zone, found only in the ocean's trenches and named after Hades, the Greek god of the underworld. Whoever named these floors was not selling holiday rentals.

title: The Twilight Zone
objective: After this level you can describe the nightly rise of deep-sea animals.
summary: Every night, twilight-zone animals swim up to feed and sink again at dawn: the largest animal migration on Earth. In WWII, sonar mistook them for the sea floor.

cards.headline: In World War II, sonar found a sea floor that rose every night.
cards.body: Navy operators hunting submarines watched the "bottom" sit deep by day, then float up near the surface after dark. The sea floor doesn't commute. So what did?

cards.headline: A living false bottom
cards.body: The "floor" was alive: a thick crowd of twilight-zone fish, squid, plankton and other animals. As darkness falls, they swim up to feed near the surface, then sink back down at daybreak. It happens every 24 hours, all around the world, and it's the largest animal migration on Earth. Every sunset, rush hour starts.

cards.headline: Why wait for dark?
cards.body: Remember Level 51: the twilight zone gets only a dim glow from above. Predators there hunt by looking up for the outline of prey against that glow. Rising only at night may help the migrators avoid becoming that outline. Dinner is worth the commute only after the lights go out.

mascot.line: Quadrillions of fish, and not one of them has ever been on a menu I've read.

cards.fact: The twilight zone may hold more fish, by weight, than all the rest of the ocean combined.
cards.context: The most common of them may be the bristlemouth, a small fish thought to be the most abundant animal with a backbone on Earth, possibly numbering in the quadrillions. The most common vertebrate on the planet is a fish you've probably never heard of.

title: Living Light
objective: After this level you can explain animals that make their own light.
summary: Bioluminescence is light from a chemical reaction. Three quarters of Monterey Bay animals can glow, mostly blue, to escape, hide or hunt.

cards.headline: Some deep-sea shrimp throw up light at their enemies.
cards.body: Grab one, and it releases a cloud of glowing fluid from near its mouth. Gross? Yes. Useful? The glow probably confuses the attacker. Down here, light is a weapon, a disguise and a dinner bell.

cards.headline: Light from a chemical reaction
cards.body: That glow is bioluminescence: light made by a living thing. Inside the animal, an enzyme and another chemical react and give off light. Different species use different chemicals, which suggests living light evolved many separate times. Nature kept reinventing the flashlight.

cards.fact: In one deep-sea survey, three quarters of the animals could make their own light.
cards.context: In 2017, MBARI scientists counted animals in Monterey Bay from the surface down to 4,000 m. On land, glowing animals are the exception. In the open ocean, they're the rule.

cards.headline: Why so blue?
cards.body: Remember Level 8: red light fades first underwater and blue travels deepest. So most ocean bioluminescence is blue, the color that carries best through seawater. An animal flashing red down here would mostly be signaling to nobody.

mascot.line: Turning on a light to become invisible. I'm going to be thinking about that one all day.

cards.headline: Hiding with the lights on

title: Giant Squid
objective: After this level you can describe giant and colossal squid.
summary: The giant squid, up to about 13 m, was first photographed alive in 2004. The colossal squid, the heaviest invertebrate, was first filmed alive in 2025.

cards.headline: To find the giant squid, two scientists followed its worst enemy.
cards.body: Sperm whales hunt giant squid. So Tsunemi Kubodera and Kyoichi Mori dropped a camera where sperm whales dive to feed, off Japan's Ogasawara Islands. In 2004, at about 900 m, a giant squid attacked their bait and became the first ever photographed alive in the wild.

cards.headline: Built on a giant scale
cards.body: The giant squid can reach roughly 13 m long. Its eyes grow up to 27 cm across, among the largest of any living animal. Those eyes may be an early-warning system: they could let it make out the shape of a hunting sperm whale more than 120 m away. Big eyes for a big enemy.

cards.fact: The colossal squid can weigh about 500 kg: the heaviest invertebrate on Earth.
cards.context: It lives in the cold, deep Southern Ocean. For 100 years after it was named, scientists met it mainly as remains in the stomachs of whales and seabirds. Quite a way to be known: by what ate you.

mascot.line: A hundred years of waiting, and the star turned up as a baby. Perfect casting.

cards.headline: A baby steals the show
cards.body: Then, on March 9, 2025, a team on Schmidt Ocean Institute's ship Falkor (too) filmed a colossal squid alive in its own habitat for the first time, near the South Sandwich Islands. It was a juvenile, just 30 cm long, at 600 m. The heaviest invertebrate on Earth made its screen debut at the size of a school ruler.

title: The Anglerfish
objective: After this level you can explain how the anglerfish hunts in the dark.
summary: Where food is scarce, the anglerfish saves energy: it waits with a glowing lure and a mouth of backward teeth. In some families the tiny male fuses to the female for life.

cards.headline: The anglerfish never chases dinner. Dinner comes to it.
cards.body: Anglerfish are among the most rarely seen of all deep-sea fishes. When MBARI filmed a black seadevil alive about 580 m down in 2014, it was the first video of that species at home. Here's how it makes a living where meals almost never swim by.

cards.headline: Fishing saves fuel
cards.body: Deep down, food is scarce, and swimming around searching burns energy a hunter can't spare. So the anglerfish fishes instead. Most adult females carry a lure on a "fishing rod," glowing with bacteria that live inside it. Then the anglerfish hangs in the dark and waits. Why chase when the snacks come to you?

cards.headline: One bite, no escape
cards.body: When prey drifts in to inspect the light, a huge mouth snaps shut. Its sharp teeth point backward, so nothing wriggles out, and some anglerfish have been known to swallow prey larger than themselves. When meals are this rare, you don't let one go.

mascot.line: I've heard of clingy partners, but this is something else entirely.

cards.headline: Partners for life, literally
cards.body: Finding a mate in the dark is even harder than finding food. It's the ultimate long-term relationship.

title: Whale Falls
objective: After this level you can explain what happens when a whale sinks to the sea floor.
summary: A sunken whale can feed the deep like thousands of years of marine snow: scavengers first, bone-eating worms next, then bacteria in the bones for decades.

cards.headline: One dead whale can feed the deep sea like thousands of years of snow.
cards.body: Not frozen snow: marine snow, the slow drizzle of dead plankton, waste and other bits that feeds much of the deep. Now and then something far bigger drops in. When a whale sinks, the sea floor gets a feast that can last for decades.

cards.headline: Stage one: the cleanup crew
cards.body: Within days, scavengers arrive: sleeper sharks, hagfish, rattails and tiny amphipods. They tear away the flesh, and the whale is often stripped to the bone within months. Word gets around fast when dinner is this rare.

mascot.line: No mouth, no stomach, and still the best eaters at the table. Impressive.

cards.headline: Stage two: the bone eaters
cards.body: On a dead whale nearly 2,900 m down in Monterey Canyon, found in 2002, MBARI scientists discovered worms that live on bone. In 2004 they were named Osedax, Latin for "bone devourer." They have no mouth and no stomach. Green roots reach into the bone, where bacteria help digest the fats and oils inside.

cards.headline: Stage three: power from bones
cards.body: After a year or two, the easy food is gone, but the bones are still soaked in fats and oils. Bacteria feed on them and release hydrogen sulfide, and a whole community builds on those bacteria instead of on sunlight. It can keep going for decades. The whale's last gift is its skeleton.

title: Life Without Sunlight
objective: After this level you can explain how life thrives around hydrothermal vents.
summary: At hydrothermal vents, microbes make food from hydrogen sulfide instead of sunlight. Giant tubeworms have no mouth: microbes inside them do the cooking.

cards.headline: In 1977, scientists found a crowd living where sunlight had never reached.
cards.body: Exploring the sea floor near the Galapagos Islands, they found hydrothermal vents, with animals living all around them. Every food web they knew began with sunlight. This one couldn't.

cards.headline: Food from chemicals
cards.body: Remember Level 8: below about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis. At a vent, microbes don't need it. They take hydrogen sulfide from the vent water and turn it into food. That's chemosynthesis, and tubeworms, shrimp and mussels all live on what the microbes make. Who needs the Sun when you have chemistry?

mascot.line: Think of it as a worm with a kitchen inside and a team of very tiny cooks.

cards.headline: The worm with no mouth
cards.body: Giant tubeworms can stand nearly 2 m tall, yet they have no mouth and no gut. Instead, microbes live inside their bodies and turn vent chemicals into food, which they share with the worm. The tubeworm doesn't catch its dinner. It grows it in-house.

cards.headline: Same trick, different address
cards.body: Sound familiar? Level 56's whale bones work the same way: bacteria release hydrogen sulfide, and a whole community builds on bacteria instead of sunlight. Hot vents and old bones are very different places, but the recipe is the same. Wherever the deep offers chemical energy, life moves in.

title: Deep-Sea Giants
objective: After this level you can explain why some deep-sea animals grow so large.
summary: Many deep animals outgrow their shallow relatives. Cold slows their lives, few predators trouble them, and big bodies cope better when food is scarce.

cards.headline: The pill bug in your garden has a deep-sea cousin longer than a school ruler.
cards.body: Giant isopods crawl the deep sea floor and can grow more than 30 cm long. They aren't alone: down in the cold and dark, animal after animal comes in an oversized edition. Why does the deep grow giants?

cards.headline: Supersized
cards.body: Giant isopods are much larger than their shallow-water relatives, and so are many other deep-sea animals. Scientists call it deep-sea gigantism. Remember Level 54's colossal squid, the heaviest invertebrate on Earth? It's one of the pattern's headliners.

cards.headline: Slow and steady
cards.body: Scientists aren't sure what drives it, and several causes may work together. One is the cold: chilly deep water slows animals' metabolisms, and many deep-sea creatures grow and mature very slowly. Another is that few predators bother a big, armored isopod, so it can take its time. Growing up slowly, it turns out, can mean growing up big.

mascot.line: Five years without a snack. I get grumpy after five hours.

cards.headline: A body built for lean times
cards.body: Food is scarce down here, and a big body helps. Larger animals can travel farther to find food, use energy more efficiently and store more of it. One giant isopod in a Japanese aquarium reportedly went about five years without eating. Size is the deep sea's packed lunch.

title: Undiscovered Species
objective: After this level you can explain how much of the deep sea is still unexplored.
summary: People have seen less than 0.001% of the deep seafloor. About a quarter of a million marine species are named; in one deep Pacific plain, about 90% of species had no name.

cards.headline: People have seen less than 0.001% of the deep sea floor.
cards.body: Not mapped from a ship: actually looked at, by eye or by camera. The deep ocean covers about 66% of Earth's surface, and almost all of its floor has never been seen by anyone.

cards.headline: A Rhode Island of seafloor
cards.body: A 2025 study added up about 44,000 deep-sea dives since 1958. Everything they saw of the deep floor comes to an area about the size of Rhode Island. Judging all life on land from the same share would mean studying an area about the size of Houston, Texas, and calling it the whole planet.

cards.headline: Most species have no name yet
cards.body: So it's no surprise that the ocean's guest list is unfinished. Only about a quarter of a million marine species have been documented, and millions more are thought to be waiting. The ocean's roll call has barely started.

cards.fact: In one deep Pacific plain, around 90% of the species found had no scientific name.
cards.context: A 2023 study looked at the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a plain between Hawaii and Mexico about 5,000 m down. Nine out of ten of the species recorded there were new to science. Send a camera almost anywhere deep, and it may meet strangers.

title: Checkpoint: The Deep
objective: After this level you can describe how animals survive the dark, cold and pressure of the deep.
summary: The deepest fish ever filmed swam at 8,336 m. Deep animals beat pressure by being mostly water, darkness with their own light or red bodies, and cold and hunger by going slow and big.

cards.headline: The deepest fish ever filmed was a baby.
cards.body: In 2022, a University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology team filmed a small juvenile snailfish at 8,336 m in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench off Japan. Let's use the whole chapter to explain how anything lives down there.

cards.headline: Pressure: be mostly water
cards.body: Level 9's foam cup shrank because air squeezes. Most deep-sea animals are largely water, which barely compresses, and many have no air-filled spaces, like lungs or swim bladders, to crush. Some animals even migrate 1,000 m up and down every day, through a 100-atmosphere swing, with no harm done. Their secret is having nothing to squash.

cards.headline: Darkness: make light, or vanish
cards.body: No sunlight reaches below 1,000 m, so many animals make their own: mostly blue bioluminescence, to escape, hide and hunt. Others hide by color. Red light never reaches the deep, so red animals look black and all but disappear.

cards.headline: Cold and hunger: go slow, think big
cards.body: The midnight zone holds a steady 4°C, and cold slows bodies down. Hunters like the anglerfish wait with a lure instead of chasing, many animals grow large to go farther between meals, and some neighborhoods skip sunlight entirely, living on whale bones and vent chemicals. The deep rewards patience.

title: Beaches
objective: After this level you can explain where beach sand comes from.
summary: Most beach sand is worn-down rock carried by rivers, and quartz survives best. Local sources add color: black lava, pink shells of forams, white coral ground by parrotfish.

cards.headline: Much of Hawaii's famous white sand came out of a fish.
cards.body: Not a figure of speech. A fish bit off coral, ground it up and pooped it out. Before we meet the fish, here's the ordinary way to make a beach: break rock down for a very, very long time.

cards.headline: Mountains, delivered in pieces
cards.body: Most sand starts as rock. Weathering and erosion break rocks down over thousands or even millions of years, and streams and rivers carry the pieces toward the sea, grinding them smaller on the way. Remember Level 5, where rivers carried salt from broken-down rock to the sea? The same rivers deliver sand. Quartz is hard, doesn't split easily and barely dissolves, so it outlasts other minerals and is by far the commonest mineral in sand. A tan beach is mostly quartz, tinted by iron oxide, plus feldspar: the toughest leftovers of old rock.

title: Cliffs and Sea Caves
objective: After this level you can explain how the sea carves cliffs and caves.
summary: Waves quarry cracked rock with trapped air and grind it with sand. Caves open along weak spots like fractures, and notched cliffs collapse and retreat, leaving wave-cut platforms.

cards.headline: A California sea cave runs about 370 m into solid rock.
cards.body: It's Painted Cave, on Santa Cruz Island in Channel Islands National Park, and it's the largest sea cave in California. Nobody dug it. The waves did. So how does water, of all things, tunnel into rock?

cards.headline: A hammer and sandpaper
cards.body: A breaking wave doesn't just splash. It slams into the shore and traps air in the cracks of the rock, squeezing it hard. The impact of all that water plus the compressed air can pry loose chunks of fractured rock, a process called quarrying. Waves also hurl sand and stones at the shore, grinding it down by abrasion. Remember Level 61's sand, worn from rock? Here the sea turns it back against the rock as sandpaper.

cards.headline: Find the weak spot
cards.body: Waves don't carve evenly. Most sea caves form along weaknesses in the rock, such as faults, fractures or layers of softer rock, which the waves and the sand they carry widen first. On the Channel Islands, most caves formed as waves worked along narrow fractures. Keep going long enough and a cave through a headland can become a sea arch, and when the arch collapses, it leaves a sea stack. Most sea caves start as a crack the sea found first.

mascot.line: Cliffs don't so much fall down as get their feet knocked out from under them.

cards.headline: How a cliff walks backward
cards.body: Waves erode the foot of a cliff, cutting a notch there. The rock above is left overhanging, and sooner or later it falls. The waves clear it away and cut a new notch. So the cliff retreats, and behind it is left a gently sloping rock ledge, a wave-cut platform, running from the cliff's foot out below low tide. That flat rock shelf you can walk on at low tide marks where the cliff used to stand.

title: Estuaries and Mangroves
objective: After this level you can describe where rivers meet the sea.
summary: Estuaries mix river water and seawater into brackish nurseries for young sea life. Mangrove trees stand in salty tides, shedding salt and holding the shore with their roots.

cards.headline: America's biggest estuary is a river valley the sea moved into.
cards.body: The Chesapeake Bay is the drowned valley of the Susquehanna River, flooded as the sea rose after the last ice age. Today it's not quite river and not quite sea, and that in-between water is among the most productive places on Earth.

cards.headline: Half fresh, half salt
cards.body: Where a river meets the sea, fresh water draining off the land mixes with salty seawater. The mix is called brackish water, and the place is an estuary. Living there is tricky, because the saltiness keeps shifting. Oysters cope by shutting their shells and pausing their meals when low tide leaves them in water that's too fresh. It's like eating in a kitchen where someone keeps changing the seasoning.

cards.fact: Estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems in the world.
cards.context: They filter the runoff that drains off the land, and their sheltered water is a nursery where many young animals grow up, including many of the fish people catch. No wonder they're called the nurseries of the sea.

cards.headline: Trees that stand in the sea
cards.body: On tropical coasts, many shores and estuaries are lined with mangroves: trees that grow where the tides flood in, most of them at least twice a day. They grow only at tropical and subtropical latitudes, because they can't survive freezing. Their tangled prop roots make them look like they're standing on stilts. And the salt? Some mangroves filter it out at their roots; others push it out through glands on their leaves, leaving crystals on top.

cards.headline: Roots that hold the coast
cards.body: Those roots do more than hold the tree up. They slow the tidal water, so the mud it carries settles out. They shelter fish and other animals looking for food and a hiding place from predators. And they stabilize the coastline, reducing erosion from storm surges, currents, waves and tides. A mangrove forest is a seawall that grows its own replacement parts.

title: Volcanic Islands
objective: After this level you can explain islands like Hawaii.
summary: Hawaii's islands grew over a hot spot as the Pacific Plate carried each away. Older islands to the northwest sink and erode; the next, Kamaʻehuakanaloa, is still 975 m down.

cards.headline: Hawaii's next island is already erupting, 975 m underwater.
cards.body: Kamaʻehuakanaloa, an active volcano off the coast of the Island of Hawaii, rises to about 975 m below the surface. Why would a new island grow right there, and nowhere else? Follow the chain.

cards.headline: A conveyor belt of volcanoes
cards.body: Deep below Hawaii is a hot spot that feeds volcanoes. The Pacific Plate slides over it, carrying each volcano away to the northwest while a new one grows behind it. So the islands line up by age. On the Island of Hawaii, still over the hot spot, the oldest exposed rocks are less than 0.7 million years old. On Kauaʻi, far to the northwest, they're about 5.5 million years old and deeply eroded. The youngest in the family is the one still sitting on the burner.

cards.headline: Islands that sink
cards.body: Once an island drifts off the hot spot, its volcanoes die and two slow forces take over. Its enormous weight bends Earth's almost rigid outer layer beneath it, so it sinks. Meanwhile the sea, rain and wind wear it down. The Island of Hawaii sits at the young end of a chain of more than 125 volcanoes. Toward the far end, near Midway, about 28 million years old, the old islands have dwindled to small patches of land, shoals and reefs.

cards.headline: Tomorrow's island
cards.body: Back to Kamaʻehuakanaloa. It's in a volcano's earliest stage: small eruptions, all below sea level. The USGS expects it to be millennia before it breaks the surface. When it does, it will be the newest stop on the conveyor belt, and the Island of Hawaii will begin its own slow ride northwest. No rush on the beach towels.

cards.headline: Darwin explained coral atolls before he'd seen a true coral reef.
cards.body: He worked it out on the west coast of South America, during the Beagle voyage, while thinking about how land slowly rises and sinks. His answer to the riddle of ring-shaped islands: look for the volcano that isn't there anymore.

cards.headline: Where did the island go?
cards.body: Remember Level 64: old volcanic islands sink under their own weight. Darwin's insight was that the reef doesn't have to go down with the ship. It keeps growing upward while the island sinks, so it stays near the surface as the volcano disappears below. It's slow work: barrier reefs and atolls can take from 100,000 to 30 million years to fully form.

cards.fact: In 1952, drills at Enewetak Atoll went through more than 1 km of coral before hitting volcanic rock.
cards.context: It was the first geologic drilling of an atoll, and it found the sunken volcano right where Darwin's idea said it should be. He had published his theory in 1842, so the proof took more than a century to arrive. Worth the wait.

cards.headline: Where the race is lost
cards.body: An atoll is a race: coral grows up while the island sinks. At the far northwest end of the Hawaiian chain sits Kure Atoll, the northernmost coral atoll in the world. There, cooler water slows the coral until its growth only just matches the sinking. Past Kure, the reefs can't keep up, and the chain carries on as drowned, submerged platforms. Scientists call this tipping line the Darwin Point.

title: Harbors and Ports
objective: After this level you can explain what makes a good harbor.
summary: A harbor is deep water sheltered from wind, waves and currents. Nature makes most, like drowned river valleys; people build others with breakwaters, as at Normandy in 1944.

cards.headline: In 1944, the Allies brought their own harbors to France.
cards.body: German forces had fortified the Channel ports, so for the D-Day landings the Allies built two artificial harbors in Britain and floated them to Normandy. Why go to all that trouble? Because ships full of supplies are useless without somewhere safe to unload.

cards.headline: What makes a harbor
cards.body: A harbor is water sheltered from wind, waves and currents, so ships can anchor safely and load or unload cargo and passengers. It must also be deep enough to keep ships from touching bottom, with room for them to turn and pass each other. The open sea is great for sailing and terrible for parking.

cards.headline: Harbors the sea made
cards.body: Most harbors are natural: bays, coves, fjords, lagoons and estuaries that already give shelter. Remember Level 63's Chesapeake Bay, a river valley flooded by the sea? When the ice-age glaciers melted and sea level rose, the sea flooded the lower ends of river valleys, leaving funnel-shaped inlets called rias. Sydney Harbour is a drowned river valley like that, and one of the world's finest natural harbors.

cards.headline: Harbors people build
cards.body: Where nature offers no shelter, people build it. Breakwaters, huge walls of concrete, steel and wire, are the most important part of an artificial harbor: they absorb or turn aside the incoming waves. Dredging scoops sand and sediment off the bottom to keep harbors deep enough. A harbor, in the end, is a calm spot you either find or make.

cards.fact: In June 1944, a storm wrecked one of the two Mulberry harbors within days.
cards.context: It began on June 19, and by June 22 the American harbor was destroyed. Its breakwaters had been built from sunken concrete caissons and deliberately scuttled ships. The British harbor at Arromanches survived and served the Allied armies for 10 months. Shelter, it turns out, is the whole point.

title: Seashells
objective: After this level you can explain how mollusks build their shells.
summary: A mollusk's mantle builds its shell from calcium carbonate made with seawater's building blocks, adding at the edges as it grows. Yearly bands showed one clam, Ming, was 507.

cards.headline: Scientists aged a clam by counting its shell. It was 507.
cards.body: The clam, later nicknamed Ming, was dredged off Iceland in 2006. Its shell held a year-by-year record going back five centuries. To read that record, you first need to know how a shell gets built.

cards.headline: A house made from the sea
cards.body: A mollusk's shell is made by its mantle, a layer of tissue that secretes proteins and minerals. The result is mostly calcium carbonate, with no more than about 2% protein. The building blocks, calcium and carbonate, come from the seawater around it. So a clam really is living in a house it built out of the sea.

mascot.line: Every seashell on a beach is a diary. Most of them just didn't keep it for five hundred years.

cards.headline: Growing at the edges
cards.body: A mollusk never sheds its shell, so the shell has to grow with it. It does that by adding new material around its edges. In the ocean quahog, the growth leaves one band a year, like the rings of a tree. Scientists counted Ming's bands and got 507 years, which makes it the oldest individual animal ever found, according to Guinness World Records. Its first bands went down around 1499.

cards.headline: Three layers deep
cards.body: Many shells are built in three layers: an outer skin of protein, a middle layer of calcium carbonate prisms, and a smooth inner layer. In some mollusks, that inner layer is nacre, the shimmering mother-of-pearl. Remember it: in Level 68, it turns an annoyance into a gem.

title: Pearls
objective: After this level you can explain how oysters make pearls.
summary: When an irritant gets stuck inside a mollusk, the mantle seals it in layers of shell. Nacre makes pearls shine. Farmers start cultured pearls with a bead and mantle tissue.

cards.headline: A pearl is a mollusk's way of dealing with an annoyance.
cards.body: Something gets stuck inside that it can't flush out, so it wraps it up, layer after layer. Keep wrapping, and the annoyance becomes a gem.

cards.headline: Seal it in
cards.body: The trigger is usually a tiny irritant, such as a parasite or a bit of debris, stuck in the mollusk's soft tissue where it can't be flushed out. The mantle, the same tissue that builds the shell in Level 67, coats the intruder with shell material, layer upon layer, until it's sealed inside a hard ball. The pearl isn't a present the oyster made for you. It's a quarantine.

cards.headline: Why some pearls shine
cards.body: Oysters, mussels and clams can all make pearls, but only certain mollusks coat them in nacre, the mother-of-pearl you met lining some shells. Nacre is organic secretions plus aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate, stacked like bricks and mortar. That structure makes it very strong, and it gives gem pearls their shimmer. No nacre, no sheen.

cards.headline: Pearls on purpose
cards.body: Natural pearls form without any human help. Cultured pearls are started on purpose. In the early 1890s in Japan, Mikimoto Kōkichi got pearl oysters to grow half pearls around beads he had inserted. Today a technician slips a shell bead and a small piece of mantle tissue into a host mollusk. The tissue grows into a sac around the bead and coats it with nacre, and two to five years later there's a pearl to harvest.

title: Coastal Erosion
objective: After this level you can explain how coasts wear away and how people defend them.
summary: Storms and waves move beach sand, and coasts starved of sediment retreat. Groins and seawalls can shift the loss elsewhere, softer fixes help, and sometimes people move instead.

cards.headline: In 1999, a brick lighthouse was moved about 880 m inland.
cards.body: When the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse was finished in 1870, it stood about 460 m from the ocean. By 1970, erosion had left it about 37 m from the water's edge. The lighthouse hadn't moved. The coast had.

cards.headline: Where the beach goes
cards.body: A beach is sand on the move. Breaking waves carry it along the coast, taking it from one stretch and dropping it on another, and storms are the main cause of beach erosion along many coasts. A beach also needs fresh supplies. Remember Level 61's rivers delivering sand? Coasts starved of sediment erode and migrate inland.

title: Checkpoint: Coasts and Islands
objective: After this level you can explain how waves, rivers and volcanoes shape coasts and islands.
summary: Surtsey rose off Iceland in 1963. Waves have since cut away about half of it, carving cliffs in its cracked lava, while its hard palagonite core holds on.

cards.headline: A new island rose off Iceland in 1963. The waves have been eating it since.
cards.body: Its name is Surtsey. In one young island's life you can watch almost every force from this chapter at work.

cards.fact: Surtsey lost about half its area to the waves in 35 years.
cards.context: The eruption broke the surface in November 1963 and kept going until June 1967, leaving an island of about 2.7 km². By 2002 the waves had cut it to about 1.4 km². Like Hawaii's islands in Level 64, it was built by a volcano. Unlike the Island of Hawaii, it has had no fresh lava since.

cards.headline: The weak spots go first
cards.body: The waves went after Surtsey's weak spots first, just like the caves of Level 62. In the southwest, where the lava was badly cracked, they broke down a strip of land up to 650 m wide and cut sea cliffs up to 75 m high. Elsewhere, the lava shielded the loose volcanic ash behind it. Cracks first, solid rock last.

mascot.line: An island that's shrinking on schedule. Geologists get to watch the whole show.

cards.headline: The core that stays
cards.body: Surtsey's heart is palagonite tuff, volcanic ash hardened into rock, and it stands up to the sea far better than loose ash or cracked lava. Researchers expect that after about 160 years only that core will be left, ringed by steep cliffs. Volcanoes build islands. Waves decide how long they last.

title: The Arctic Ocean
objective: After this level you can describe the Arctic Ocean.
summary: The Arctic is the smallest, shallowest ocean, almost ringed by land. Nansen's Fram showed its center is deep sea. Rivers give it a fresh, light top layer that helps ice grow.

cards.headline: In 1893, an explorer froze his own ship into the Arctic ice. On purpose.
cards.body: Fridtjof Nansen built the Fram to ride the ice, then let the frozen sea carry it. What he learned on that slow ride tells you what the Arctic Ocean really is.

cards.headline: An ocean with walls
cards.body: Remember Level 3's smallest ocean? That's the Arctic, and it's still about 1.5 times the size of the United States. North America, Eurasia and Greenland almost completely encircle it, so it's the one ocean that is nearly landlocked. For most of the year, ice covers almost all of it. Picture a huge pond, walled in by continents, with a lid on.

mascot.line: Park your ship in the ice and wait three years. Patience is an underrated research tool.

cards.headline: The ship that rode the ice
cards.body: Nansen froze the Fram into the pack ice north of Siberia and waited. For about three years the drifting ice carried the ship across the Arctic. Along the way he found that the middle of the Arctic, the Polar Basin, is deep ocean, not hidden land. The ice at the top of the world is a lid on water, and the lid moves.

cards.fact: The Arctic Ocean averages only about 987 m deep.
cards.context: That's roughly a quarter of the whole ocean's average from Level 2, about 3,700 m. So the smallest ocean is also the shallowest of the five. Small, shallow and wrapped in land: now look at what the land pours into it.

cards.headline: A fresh lid
cards.body: The Arctic holds only about 1% of the ocean's water, yet it receives about 11% of all the river water reaching the sea. Pacific water and rivers in Russia and Canada give it a cold, fresher top layer. Remember Level 6: less salty water is less dense, so it floats on top. That light, fresh lid helps more sea ice grow in the Arctic than around Antarctica.

title: Sea Ice
objective: After this level you can explain how sea ice forms and melts.
summary: Seawater freezes at about −1.8 °C, as frazil, then grease or pancake ice. Growing ice squeezes out salt, which sinks. Ice grows in winter, melts in summer, poles in turn.

cards.headline: Old sea ice is nearly fresh, even though it froze out of the salty sea.
cards.body: So where did the salt go? Follow the ice from its first crystals to its summer melt, and you'll find out.

cards.headline: Colder than freezing
cards.body: Fresh water freezes at 0 °C, but salt gets in the way, so seawater has to get colder: polar seawater starts to freeze at about −1.8 °C. The first ice is a scatter of tiny needle-like crystals called frazil. In calm water they join into a smooth, oily-looking film called grease ice. In rough water they bump together into round, slushy pancakes. Yes, pancake ice is its real name.

cards.headline: Squeezing out the salt
cards.body: As the crystals grow, they push the salt out. Some gets trapped between them in tiny pockets of very salty liquid called brine, which is why new ice is salty. Over the years that brine drains away, so ice four or more years old is nearly free of it. The sea keeps the salt; the ice keeps the water.

mascot.line: Ice on top, salt heading down. Even freezing the sea gets sorted by density.

cards.fact: The salt that sea ice pushes out makes the water below denser, so it sinks.
cards.context: Remember Level 6: cold, salty water is dense. The water under freezing ice is both. So while the ice grows on top, heavy, salty water slides away underneath. A freezing polar sea is also a sinking one.

cards.headline: Ice that comes and goes
cards.body: Sea ice grows through the winter and melts through the summer. In the Arctic it usually peaks in March and shrinks to its smallest in September, and on average only about a third of the late-winter ice survives the melt. Around Antarctica the seasons are flipped, so its ice usually peaks in September. When one pole is melting, the other is freezing.

title: Icebergs
objective: After this level you can explain why most of an iceberg is underwater.
summary: Icebergs are chunks of glacier or ice shelf, frozen fresh water from snow. Ice is only about 9% less dense than water, so about 90% of a berg floats underwater.

cards.headline: The part of an iceberg you can see is only about a tenth of it.
cards.body: About 90% hangs out of sight below the waterline. To see why, start where every iceberg starts: on land.

cards.headline: Born on land
cards.body: An iceberg isn't frozen seawater. It's a piece of a glacier or ice shelf that broke off and floated away, a break called calving. Glaciers are built from snow that piled up long enough to turn to ice, so an iceberg is frozen fresh water. Level 72's sea ice freezes in the ocean; an iceberg only ends up there. It's land ice gone to sea.

cards.headline: Greenland's iceberg factory
cards.body: Most of the icebergs that drift into North Atlantic shipping lanes come from the tidewater glaciers on Greenland's west coast, where the ice meets the sea. After breaking off, a berg takes 1 to 3 years to drift south into the lanes. Slow travelers, and not the kind you can hurry along.

mascot.line: Next time someone says 'the tip of the iceberg', you can tell them it's about a tenth.

cards.headline: Why ice floats low
cards.body: When water freezes, its molecules lock into an orderly lattice that holds them further apart, so ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water. That's why ice cubes float in your glass. But it's only a little lighter, so an iceberg floats low: about 90% of it sits below the waterline. The tip of the iceberg really is just the tip.

title: The Southern Ocean
objective: After this level you can describe the ocean around Antarctica and its life.
summary: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, Earth's largest wind-driven current, circles Antarctica and walls off the Southern Ocean. Its fish cope with antifreeze and, in icefish, blood with no hemoglobin.

cards.headline: Some fish in the Southern Ocean have no red blood cells at all.
cards.body: And they live in water cold enough to freeze the sea. To see how they manage, start with the current that fences their ocean in.

cards.headline: An ocean fenced by a current
cards.body: Remember Level 3: the Southern Ocean is the one defined by a current, with its northern edge at 60° south. That current is the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the largest wind-driven current on Earth. It flows west to east all the way around Antarctica, the only current that circles the planet, linking the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans. It also works as a barrier, keeping the Southern Ocean apart from the waters to its north.

mascot.line: Pale blood, a huge heart and freezing water. The icefish skipped the rulebook and is doing fine.

cards.fact: Antarctic icefish have no red blood cells and no hemoglobin.
cards.context: Hemoglobin is the protein that carries oxygen in your blood and makes it red. Icefish manage without it: they have bigger hearts and gill blood vessels, pumping extra blood to pull enough oxygen from the oxygen-rich Antarctic water. Most of the 16 icefish species live in the Antarctic.

cards.headline: Blood with antifreeze
cards.body: Level 72's seawater starts freezing at about −1.8 °C, and a fish swimming in it needs a way not to freeze too. In the late 1960s, biologist Arthur DeVries found the answer in Antarctic notothenioid fishes: antifreeze proteins that bind to ice crystals in their blood and keep the fish from freezing. The fish makes its own antifreeze, and carries it everywhere.

title: Krill
objective: After this level you can explain why tiny krill matter so much.
summary: Antarctic krill, about 5 cm long, may have the largest biomass of any wild animal species. They feed penguins, whales and fish, and their young winter under the sea ice.

cards.headline: An animal about 5 cm long may be the heaviest wild species on Earth.
cards.body: Not one of them, of course. All of them together. Meet Antarctic krill, and find out why so much of the Southern Ocean runs on them.

cards.fact: Antarctic krill may have the largest total biomass of any wild animal species.
cards.context: The best estimate for all of them together is about 379 million tonnes. Each one is a small, see-through, shrimp-like crustacean about 5 cm long, and they live in vast, dense swarms. Tiny, but never alone.

cards.headline: Everybody's lunch
cards.body: Krill graze on microscopic algae, and they are the main food for many of the Southern Ocean's bigger animals: penguins, whales and fish. That makes them the link between the smallest living things and the biggest. The blue whale, the largest animal known to have lived, eats almost nothing but krill, up to 6 tons of them a day. The giant runs on the tiny.

mascot.line: A roof of ice with dinner stuck to the ceiling. Honestly, not a bad place to grow up.

cards.headline: A nursery under the ice
cards.body: Winter is the hard part. Young krill spend it under the sea ice, where the rough, complex underside of the ice gives them shelter from predators and access to food. Scientists call winter sea ice the krill's nursery and feeding ground. Remember Level 72's ice that grows every winter? For a young krill, that's the roof over its head.

title: Whales of the Poles
objective: After this level you can describe the whales that feed in polar seas.
summary: Humpbacks commute: summer feasts in polar seas, winter calving in the tropics, up to about 8,000 km away. Only belugas, narwhals and bowheads stay in the Arctic all year.

cards.headline: Some whales swim about 8,000 km just to reach their summer meal.
cards.body: Others never leave the ice at all. The polar seas have two kinds of whale: the commuters and the locals.

cards.headline: The commuters
cards.body: Humpback whales spend the summer in cold, food-rich polar waters, straining Level 75's krill and small fish through their baleen. In winter they head for tropical breeding grounds to mate and have their calves, and some populations swim about 8,000 km between the two. The fat they build up in summer carries them through the winter. They eat in the cold and raise their young in the warm.

cards.headline: Summer visitors, year-round locals
cards.body: The Arctic gets summer visitors too: humpbacks, minkes and fin whales arrive from the south and leave again as it cools. But only three whales live in the Arctic all year: the beluga, the narwhal and the bowhead. The narwhal's famous tusk is actually an enlarged left tooth. One very long tooth.

mascot.line: Opening a skylight with your head. Not recommended without a reinforced skull.

cards.fact: A bowhead whale can break through sea ice about 20 cm thick with its head.
cards.context: Its large, reinforced skull makes a handy icebreaker when it needs a breath. Under its skin sits the thickest blubber of any whale, about 43 to 48 cm. And it's built to last: studies suggest bowheads may live more than 200 years. Blubber, a hard head and a very long life: made for the ice.

title: Seals on the Ice
objective: After this level you can describe the seals that live on polar ice.
summary: Seals under ice must keep breathing holes open: Weddell seals rasp with their teeth, ringed seals with their claws. The ice is also home: nursery, hunting ground and krill buffet.

cards.headline: Imagine living under a frozen ceiling, when you need to breathe air.
cards.body: That's life for the seals of the polar ice. They breathe through cracks and holes in it, so every seal needs a way to keep a window open. The Arctic and the Antarctic came up with two very different tools.

cards.headline: Open wide
cards.body: Weddell seals live farther south than any other mammal that stays in Antarctica all year, breathing through cracks and holes in the ice even in the winter dark. When a hole freezes over, the seal rasps it open again with its canine and incisor teeth. Over a lifetime, the teeth can wear down until the seal can no longer feed or keep its holes open. Its teeth are its ice pick.

cards.headline: Claws and snow caves
cards.body: In the Arctic, ringed seals use their sharp claws instead, keeping breathing holes open through ice that can be about 1.8 m thick or more. They give birth and nurse their pups on the ice, in lairs covered by snow. They're the smallest and most common Arctic seal, and the main prey of polar bears, which spend much of their time on the sea ice hunting them.

mascot.line: Crabeater, eats no crabs. Somewhere a naturalist is quietly blushing.

cards.fact: Crabeater seals don't eat crabs. They eat krill.
cards.context: Their teeth have extra projections that work like a sieve: gulp seawater, strain out Level 75's krill. They spend their whole lives on the pack ice around Antarctica, resting and breeding on it, and they're the most abundant seal in the Southern Ocean. Whoever named them wasn't watching lunch.

title: Melting Ice
objective: After this level you can explain how warming changes polar seas.
summary: September Arctic ice is shrinking about 12% per decade; the IPCC finds human influence the main driver. Antarctic ice had no clear trend, then record lows. Less ice means more heat and less habitat.

cards.headline: The 20 smallest Arctic ice minimums on record all came in the last 20 years.
cards.body: NSIDC said so in September 2026: every year from 2007 to 2026. Here's how the polar seas are changing, and why it matters to what lives there.

cards.fact: September Arctic sea ice is shrinking by about 12% per decade.
cards.context: Satellites have measured it since 1979, compared with the 1981-2010 average. NASA puts the rate at 12.2% per decade; NSIDC's September 2026 analysis puts it at 11.8% for 1979-2026. The record low still belongs to 2012. Some years dip less than others, but the trend points one way.

cards.headline: What the IPCC concluded
cards.body: In its 2021 report, the IPCC found human influence very likely the main driver of the Arctic's sea ice loss: about 40% less in September between 1979-1988 and 2010-2019. It projects the Arctic is likely to be practically ice-free in September at least once before 2050, in all five scenarios it considered.

cards.headline: The south is different
cards.body: Antarctic sea ice has told a different story. The IPCC found no significant trend from 1979 to 2020, because different regions changed in opposite directions. Then in 2023, the Antarctic winter maximum was the lowest in the satellite record, more than a million square km below the previous record. The IPCC has low confidence in how Antarctic sea ice will change.

mascot.line: White ice bounces sunlight away; dark water soaks it up. That one swap drives a lot of this story.

cards.headline: Less ice, more heat, fewer homes
cards.body: Losing ice feeds itself. Sea ice reflects 50 to 70% of sunlight; open ocean reflects only about 6% and absorbs the rest, so the water warms and more ice melts. For animals, the ice is home. Loss of sea ice and its snow is the main threat to Level 77's ringed seals, and scientists warn that ice decline could affect Level 75's krill.

title: Checkpoint: Polar Seas
objective: After this level you can describe the ice and life of the Arctic and Southern Oceans.
summary: The Arctic is an ocean ringed by land; Antarctica is land ringed by ocean. So Arctic ice has lasted years while most Antarctic ice melts within one, and each pole's life fits its ice.

cards.headline: The poles are mirror images: an ocean ringed by land, and land ringed by ocean.
cards.body: That single flip shapes their ice, their water and their life. Let's swap between the poles one more time, with everything this chapter taught.

cards.headline: Why the south's ice is younger
cards.body: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, so its ice is hemmed in, and ice that survives summers, 2 to 4 m thick, has been more common there. Antarctica is a continent surrounded by ocean. Nothing stops its sea ice drifting north until it melts, so most is less than a year old and usually 1 to 2 m thick. Same frozen seawater, very different lives.

cards.headline: Ice from sea, ice from land
cards.body: Put it together. Sea ice freezes from seawater and squeezes out its salt; icebergs are frozen fresh water from glaciers, built from snow. Ice is only about 9% less dense than water, which is why both float and a berg hides most of itself. And under the southern sea ice, young krill spend the winter. The ice isn't just scenery; it's the floor, the roof and the nursery of the polar seas.

title: Early Sailors
objective: After this level you can describe the first long ocean voyages.
summary: Long before Europeans crossed it, Lapita and Polynesian voyagers settled the Pacific in double-hulled canoes loaded with crops and animals.

cards.headline: When Europeans sailed into the Pacific, its islands were already home.
cards.body: By the 1500s, almost every island out there that could support people had been settled for hundreds of years. So who crossed the open Pacific first, and in what?

events.label: People reach Australia and New Guinea across short stretches of sea

cards.headline: A trail of broken pots
cards.body: How do we know who went first? They left pottery behind. Archaeologists call the culture Lapita, after a site in New Caledonia where its distinctive pottery was found. From New Guinea it spread east as far as Fiji, Tonga and Samoa. At that eastern edge, in Tonga and Samoa, Polynesian culture grew up. Broken pots, it turns out, make excellent footprints.

mascot.line: Seeds, piglets and a map in your head. That's not a cruise, that's a moving day.

cards.headline: A farm on two hulls
cards.body: The voyaging canoe was two hulls lashed together with crossbeams, a deck between them, and sails woven from coconut or pandanus leaves. On board went taro, breadfruit, bananas and coconuts, plus pigs, dogs and chickens. You don't pack a farm for a fishing trip. These were planned voyages to settle new land.

cards.fact: Voyaging canoes sailed sea roads of more than 3,200 km.
cards.context: The longest ran between Hawaiʻi and Tahiti. Remember Level 3: the Pacific is by far the largest ocean, big enough to hold all the continents. Its settlers crossed it in canoes, one island at a time.

title: Steering by the Stars
objective: After this level you can explain how sailors navigated by the stars.
summary: Wayfinders steer by where stars rise and set. A star's height gives latitude; longitude needed a clock, until Harrison's H4.

cards.headline: Hawaiian navigators steer by about 220 stars kept in their heads.
cards.body: No compass, no clock. Navigator Nainoa Thompson memorizes where each star comes up out of the sea and where it goes down. So what can the stars tell a sailor, and what can't they?

cards.headline: A compass made of horizon
cards.body: The Hawaiian star compass, developed by Nainoa Thompson, divides the horizon into 32 houses: the places where the Sun, stars, Moon and planets rise and set. It isn't an object at all. It lives in the navigator's memory. Watch a known star rise in its house and you know your heading. Thompson learned wayfinding from Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Satawal in Micronesia.
cards.callout: 32 houses on the horizon, carried in memory

cards.headline: How high tells you how far
cards.body: Stars also give you latitude: how far north or south you are. European sailors used the height of the Sun or the pole star, measuring its angle above the horizon with an instrument such as a sextant. Wayfinders read the same clue. Sailing north toward Hawaiʻi, the Southern Cross sits lower each night, and at Hawaiʻi's latitude the gap between its top and bottom stars matches the gap from the bottom star to the horizon.

mascot.line: The stars answer north and south for free. East and west cost Britain a prize and a very patient clockmaker.

cards.headline: East and west needed a clock
cards.body: Longitude was the hard part: there's no natural starting line. But Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so each hour between your local time and home time means 15° of longitude. You just needed a clock that kept home time at sea, and pendulum clocks were useless on a rolling ship. Britain's 1714 Longitude Act offered rewards. John Harrison, a self-taught clockmaker, built H4, trialled on a voyage to Jamaica in 1761. Where am I? First ask: what time is it at home?

title: The Challenger Expedition
objective: After this level you can describe the first great scientific voyage around the ocean.
summary: HMS Challenger (1872-1876) swapped guns for labs, sounded the deep with rope and found more than 4,700 new species, founding oceanography.

cards.headline: In the 1800s, many scientists doubted anything could live in the deep sea.
cards.body: Too much pressure, too cold, too dark. In the 1840s the naturalist Edward Forbes argued that life stopped a few hundred meters down. In 1872 a British warship set out to check.

cards.headline: A warship full of laboratories
cards.body: The Royal Navy took 15 of HMS Challenger's 17 guns out and turned the space into laboratories and workrooms, making it the first dedicated oceanographic research vessel. It left England in December 1872 and spent three and a half years at sea, crossing the Atlantic, Pacific and Southern Oceans. Fewer cannons, more science.

cards.headline: Measuring the deep with rope
cards.body: How do you measure water you can't see the bottom of? Challenger's crew lowered a weighted rope until it hit the sea floor, and the ship carried dredging ropes more than 7 km long. In 1875, in the Mariana Trench, one sounding reached 4,475 fathoms (8,184 m), the deepest then known. That trench's deepest spot is now called Challenger Deep, named for a later survey ship, Challenger II, in 1951. Level 2 put it at about 11 km.

cards.fact: Challenger found more than 4,700 new species.
cards.context: Remember Level 8: below 1,000 m there's no sunlight at all. Challenger showed that life exists anyway, under extreme pressure and in total darkness. Its results filled a 50-volume report that took 23 years to compile, and the voyage is credited with giving birth to oceanography.

title: Diving Helmets
objective: After this level you can explain how early divers breathed underwater.
summary: Diving bells trapped air, then barrels and pumps refilled it. Siebe's copper helmet, fed by a hose from the surface, made hard-hat diving standard.

cards.headline: The first way to breathe underwater was to take the air down in a bell.
cards.body: Early diving bells were containers open only at the bottom, lowered with air trapped inside; Aristotle mentioned a simple one. The catch: a plain bell couldn't keep a diver breathing for more than a few minutes.

cards.headline: Fresh air, delivered
cards.body: Edmond Halley, who ran a diving company salvaging shipwrecks, fixed that by sending fresh air down in barrels, while used air escaped through a stopcock in the top. In the late 18th century, engineer John Smeaton fitted an air pump to a bell. And remember Level 9: water barely squeezes, but air does, and pressure climbs one atmosphere every 10 m. The deeper the bell, the harder the sea leaned on its air.

cards.headline: A helmet on a hose
cards.body: In the 1830s, Augustus Siebe developed a copper helmet sealed to a waterproof suit. Air was pumped down a hose from the surface, a valve let breathed air out, and only the diver's hands met the water. In 1840 his suits were used to clear the wreck of HMS Royal George, and the design caught on. The diver no longer lived in a bell. The bell came along as a hat.

mascot.line: Every breath depended on someone cranking a wheel upstairs. Be very nice to your crew.

cards.fact: The US Navy's Mark V hard-hat helmet served from 1916 to 1984.
cards.context: The hard hat had staying power, but it had a price. Crews on deck turned wheels to pump the diver's air, and the diver wore heavy weights to stay down. The hose was a lifeline, and a leash.

title: Scuba
objective: After this level you can explain how scuba gear works.
summary: The 1943 Aqua-Lung's regulator gives tank air at the water's pressure. Divers must exhale while rising and ascend slowly to avoid the bends.

cards.headline: A snorkel won't let you breathe even a meter down, however long it is.
cards.body: Try it from about a meter under and the water pressure beats your lungs: you can't pull surface air down the tube. To breathe deeper, you need air that's already pressurized, more so the deeper you go.

cards.headline: Air on demand
cards.body: In 1943 Jacques-Yves Cousteau and engineer Émile Gagnan built the Aqua-Lung, adapting a gas regulator Gagnan had designed. Its demand regulator releases tank air only when you breathe in, at the pressure of the water around you. No hose, no pump crew. It was the first truly self-contained underwater breathing apparatus: scuba.

cards.headline: Breathe out on the way up
cards.body: Scuba air is squeezed to match the water, so it grows as you rise. Remember Level 9: at 10 m the pressure is double the surface. Fill your lungs there, rise without breathing out, and that air doubles in volume, enough to overinflate and rupture your lungs. Holding your breath on the way up is the most common cause of that injury, so the rule is simple: keep breathing out.

mascot.line: Go down at your leisure, come up like a sloth. Your nitrogen will thank you.

cards.headline: The bends
cards.body: Pressure has a slower trick. Each breath at depth packs in more gas, and the extra nitrogen builds up in your blood and tissues. Rise too fast and it forms bubbles, like a shaken soda opened too quickly: decompression sickness, or the bends. Divers avoid it by limiting depth and time, rising slowly, and often pausing a few minutes about 4.5 m below the surface.

title: Submarines
objective: After this level you can explain how submarines dive and surface.
summary: Submarines flood ballast tanks to dive and blow them with compressed air to rise. Nautilus went nuclear and under the Pole; Alvin carries scientists deep.

cards.headline: To dive, a submarine lets the sea in.
cards.body: A submarine design from 1747 even used goatskin bags: fill them with water to sink, force the water out to rise. Today's submarines play the same trick with tanks.

cards.headline: Ballast tanks
cards.body: Submarines and submersibles control their buoyancy with ballast tanks. To submerge, they flood the tanks with seawater, swapping air for water until the craft sinks. To come back up, they blow the tanks clear with stored compressed air, or drop ballast weights, and float again. Get the balance of water and air right and a craft can hover at any depth.

cards.headline: Nautilus goes under the Pole
cards.body: USS Nautilus, commissioned in 1954, was the world's first nuclear-powered submarine, and a nuclear sub could stay fully submerged at high speed indefinitely. On August 3, 1958, Nautilus became the first ship to pass under the North Pole, sliding beneath the Arctic ice. The top of the world, crossed from underneath.

title: The Deepest Dive
objective: After this level you can describe the dives to the deepest point in the ocean.
summary: In 1960 Trieste, lifted by gasoline and sunk by iron, reached Challenger Deep. Cameron dove solo in 2012; Vescovo went down four times in 2019.

cards.headline: On January 23, 1960, two men sank to the deepest place in the ocean.
cards.body: Jacques Piccard and US Navy Lieutenant Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of Challenger Deep, about 11 km down. Nobody went back to the bottom until 2012. How do you get down there, and home again?

cards.headline: A balloon in the sea
cards.body: Trieste hung from a huge float filled with gasoline. Gasoline is lighter than water, so it gave lift, and it barely compresses, so the deep couldn't crush the float the way it shrank Level 9's foam cup. To sink, Trieste carried heavy iron pellets held by electromagnets. To come home, it simply let them go.

cards.headline: Twenty minutes at the bottom
cards.body: The trip down took nearly five hours. Trieste reported about 10,916 m, the crew stayed about 20 minutes, then dropped ballast for a rise of more than three hours. HMS Challenger's rope had found 8,184 m there in 1875. Use Level 9's rule and divide by 10: the water was pressing with roughly 1,090 atmospheres.

title: Satellites Watch the Sea
objective: After this level you can explain how satellites measure the ocean.
summary: Radar altimeters time echoes to measure sea height to a few centimeters. Other sensors read temperature and color, and Argo floats measure below.

cards.headline: Sea level isn't level: the Pacific sits about 20 cm above the Atlantic.
cards.body: Pacific water is usually warmer and fresher, so it's less dense and stands a little taller, just as Level 6's layers would predict. But how do you measure a 20 cm hill spread across an ocean? From space.

cards.headline: Timing echoes from orbit
cards.body: Sonar times a sound pulse's echo underwater. A satellite radar altimeter does the same with radio pulses: it bounces them off the sea and times how long they take to come back. Since TOPEX/Poseidon launched in 1992, a line of these satellites has flown the same track, repeating it every ten days. They measure sea level to within a few centimeters for 90% of the ocean.

cards.headline: Heat and color from above
cards.body: Other satellite sensors read the temperature of the sea surface, which reveals cold upwelling water and warm currents such as the Gulf Stream. Ocean-color sensors spot blooms of algae, the plankton whose chlorophyll can tint the sea green (Level 7), and help forecast where a bloom will drift.

mascot.line: Satellites above, floats below, and a Greek myth holding them together. Oceanographers love a good pun.

cards.headline: Robots below the surface
cards.body: Satellites only see the sea's skin, so the Argo program sends down thousands of robot floats. Each drifts about 1 km deep. Every ten days it sinks to 2 km, then rises, measuring temperature and salinity, and radios its data to a satellite. It changes depth by pumping oil in and out of an outside bladder: Level 87's ballast trick. Argo is named for Jason's ship, because the floats work with the Jason satellites.

title: Fishing
objective: After this level you can explain how fishing feeds the world.
summary: Fishing and fish farming made a record 195 million tonnes of aquatic animals in 2024. The wild catch has been flat since the 1980s; farms took the lead in 2022.

cards.headline: Farms now raise more seafood than all the world's fishing boats catch.
cards.body: For almost all of history, eating from the sea meant hunting wild animals. In 2022 that quietly changed. Follow the world's seafood from the net to the farm and see why.

cards.fact: In 2024, fishing and fish farming produced a record 195 million tonnes of aquatic animals.
cards.context: That's fish, plus shellfish like mussels and shrimp, according to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Shared out, it's enough for about 21 kg per person on Earth, as measured in 2023. That's roughly a packed suitcase of seafood for each of us, every year.

cards.headline: Protein for billions
cards.body: For 3.1 billion people, fish and other aquatic foods supply at least a fifth of all the animal protein they eat, FAO reports. That's not a garnish or a treat; it's dinner, week in and week out. For them, the ocean is less a view than a pantry.

cards.headline: The wild catch hit a ceiling
cards.body: Here's the twist. Since the late 1980s, the world's wild catch has barely grown, staying between about 86 and 94 million tonnes a year. Most of it comes from the sea: 80 of the 92 million tonnes caught in 2024. More people, more appetite, roughly the same catch. The ocean can only hand over so much.

cards.headline: Down on the fish farm
cards.body: So the growth came from farming. Aquaculture means raising fish, shellfish and other water animals, and in 2022 it produced more of them than all capture fisheries for the first time. By 2024, farms made 103 million tonnes, about 53% of the total. It's the switch from hunting to farming, happening at sea.

title: Overfishing
objective: After this level you can explain overfishing and how fisheries recover.
summary: Overfishing collapsed Newfoundland's cod: a 1992 ban meant for two years lasted 32. About 62% of stocks are fished sustainably, and swordfish show recovery works.

cards.headline: In 1992, Canada closed its biggest cod fishery for two years. It took 32.
cards.body: The fish were northern cod off Newfoundland. How does a sea full of fish run short, and what does it take to bring the fish back?

cards.headline: Faster than they can breed
cards.body: Overfishing means catching fish faster than the population can replace itself. NOAA puts it more precisely: fishing above the rate that gives the biggest catch a stock can sustain. Newfoundland's cod were overfished for decades, until on July 2, 1992, Canada banned commercial cod fishing, costing about 19,000 jobs directly. The pause was expected to last two years. A cautious commercial fishery reopened only in 2024. A sea can be emptied far faster than it refills.

cards.fact: In 2023, about 62% of assessed marine fish stocks were fished within sustainable levels.
cards.context: So roughly three stocks in eight were overfished, FAO reports. Count by catch instead, though, and about 73% of landings came from sustainable stocks, because the biggest stocks tend to be the best managed. Most of the fish actually landed come from healthy stocks; a big minority of stocks are in trouble.

mascot.line: Fish turn out to be excellent at comebacks. They mostly need us to stop interrupting.

cards.headline: How swordfish came back
cards.body: By the late 1990s, the average swordfish caught in US waters weighed about 41 kg, down from about 113 kg in the 1960s. Under an international rebuilding plan from 1999, countries cut catches and closed grounds to protect young swordfish. In 2009 the North Atlantic stock was declared rebuilt, a year ahead of target. It's not a one-off: by 2023, NOAA counted 50 US fish stocks rebuilt since 2000.

title: Shipping
objective: After this level you can explain how most goods cross the ocean.
summary: Around 80% of international trade by volume goes by sea, made cheap by containers from 1956. Ships make about 2.9% of emissions, and a net-zero plan is contested.

cards.headline: Four in five tonnes of goods traded between countries travel by ship.
cards.body: Not by plane, not by truck: by sea. How did the ocean become the world's main freight road, and what does all that hauling cost the climate?

cards.headline: The world's freight road
cards.body: UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) estimates that around 80% of the volume of international trade in goods is carried by sea. Remember Level 1: it's one connected ocean, so the same water road links coasts on every continent. Ships don't need a road built for them. The ocean already is one.

cards.headline: The box that changed everything
cards.body: In 1956, trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean sent his ship Ideal X from Newark to Houston carrying 58 metal containers. Instead of loading loose cargo piece by piece, dockworkers could lift whole boxes. Loading the old way cost more than $5.80 a ton; loading McLean's containers cost about 16 cents. A plain steel box made the ocean cheap to cross.

cards.headline: Ships and the climate
cards.body: All that hauling burns fuel. The International Maritime Organization (IMO), the UN's shipping agency, estimated that shipping made about 2.9% of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions in 2018. In 2023 its members set a goal of net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. Agreeing on the goal turned out to be the easy part.

cards.headline: A fight over the fuel bill
cards.body: In April 2025, IMO members approved a Net-Zero Framework: a fuel standard plus a price on emissions. The EU, Brazil and Pacific island nations backed it. The United States called it a global carbon tax and opposed it, as did Saudi Arabia. In October 2025, members voted 57 to 49 to delay adopting it by a year. The ocean's freight road is also a negotiating table.

title: Energy From the Sea
objective: After this level you can explain offshore wind and oil.
summary: Offshore wells gave nearly 30% of the world's crude oil in 2015. Offshore wind began at Vindeby in 1991; floating turbines reach deep water, and fishers worry about space.

cards.headline: In 1991, Denmark put 11 wind turbines in the sea.
cards.body: Vindeby was the world's first offshore wind farm. Today the sea yields both oil and wind power. Why go to all the trouble of building out on the waves?

cards.headline: Oil under the sea floor
cards.body: In 2015, offshore wells in more than 50 countries supplied nearly 30% of the world's crude oil, the US Energy Information Administration reports. Most comes from shallow water, which is cheaper and easier to drill. But companies keep drilling deeper, notably off Brazil and in the Gulf of Mexico. Nearly a third of the world's oil comes from under the sea.

cards.headline: Why wind goes to sea
cards.body: Winds at sea are strong and consistent, says the US Department of Energy,. And offshore wind farms can sit near crowded coastal cities that need the power. Vindeby's 11 turbines proved the idea in 1991. The sea offers what a wind turbine wants most: room and a steady breeze.

cards.headline: Turbines that float
cards.body: Most offshore turbines stand on foundations fixed to the sea floor, which works only in fairly shallow water. Yet about two-thirds of US offshore wind potential lies over water too deep for that. The answer: turbines mounted on floating platforms. If you can't reach the bottom, float.

cards.headline: Who shares the water?
cards.body: The sea is already a workplace. For fishers, especially trawl and dredge boats, the worry is being pushed off traditional grounds, NOAA Fisheries notes. It also notes that sea life may cluster around turbine foundations, a reef effect. Energy developers and fishers are still working out how to share the same patch of ocean.

title: Ocean Pollution
objective: After this level you can explain the main kinds of ocean pollution.
summary: About 80% of ocean pollution comes from land, mostly as runoff. Fertilizer feeds dead zones, 19 to 23 million tonnes of plastic leak in yearly, and spills add oil.

cards.headline: Most of what pollutes the sea never went near a boat.
cards.body: NOAA says about 80% of the pollution reaching the ocean comes from the land. A drip of engine oil, a sprinkle of fertilizer, a wrapper in a storm drain. Follow a few of those journeys to the sea.

cards.headline: Death by a thousand drips
cards.body: Much of it is runoff: rain washing pollution off many small sources, like cars, farms and septic tanks, into rivers and then the sea. Millions of engines each drop a little oil on roads every day, and much of it ends up in the ocean. No single drip looks like a disaster. Together, they make the land the ocean's biggest polluter.

mascot.line: Too much food causing starvation. Nature does love an irony.

cards.headline: How fertilizer suffocates the sea
cards.body: Fertilizer feeds crops, and it feeds algae too. Every summer, nutrients from farms and cities across the Mississippi-Atchafalaya River Basin reach the Gulf of Mexico. Algae bloom, die and rot, and the rotting uses up the oxygen in the water. Fish swim away or die. That's a dead zone, and it can start on a farm far from any coast.

cards.headline: Plastic, and the occasional catastrophe
cards.body: UNEP estimates 19 to 23 million tonnes of plastic waste leak into lakes, rivers and seas every year. And sometimes pollution arrives all at once. In 2010 the Deepwater Horizon blowout killed 11 workers and spilled about 507 million liters of oil over 87 days, the largest marine oil spill in US history. Spills make the headlines; most of the mess arrives quietly, from land.

title: Protected Seas
objective: After this level you can explain marine protected areas.
summary: Countries control resources up to 200 nautical miles out; the high seas beyond gained a treaty in 2026. About 10% of the ocean is protected, and scientists debate reserves.

cards.headline: Nearly two-thirds of the ocean lies beyond any country's jurisdiction.
cards.body: So who looks after it? In January 2026, a new treaty gave the world a way. First, though: who controls which parts of the sea, and what does protecting a patch of it mean?

cards.headline: Lines on the water
cards.body: Remember Level 1: the ocean's borders are lines people drew. Here are some more. Under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a coastal country controls the fish, oil and other natural resources in its exclusive economic zone, up to 200 nautical miles (about 370 km) out. Beyond lie the high seas, which cover nearly two-thirds of the ocean.

cards.headline: Protected, partly or fully
cards.body: A marine protected area (MPA) gives part of the sea extra protection. Many still allow some fishing; the strictest, no-take reserves, ban fishing and other extraction. As of April 2026, about 10% of the ocean lay in protected areas, IUCN reports. In 2022, countries agreed to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.

cards.headline: A treaty for the high seas
cards.body: The High Seas Treaty, an agreement under the Law of the Sea convention, entered into force on January 17, 2026. It lets countries create protected areas on the high seas. There's plenty of room to fill: in April 2026, protected areas covered only about 1.66% of them.

cards.headline: Do reserves work? Two scientists disagree
cards.body: In 2018, marine ecologists Enric Sala and Sylvaine Giakoumi reviewed studies and found fish biomass in no-take reserves averaged 570% more than in unprotected waters (a corrected figure). Fisheries scientist Ray Hilborn replied that the estimate was too high, and that real protection of sea life will come from how we manage the waters that are fished. The argument is over which tool does the most good.
